TI Supporting digital competency development for adult students in
   post-secondary distance education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE adult students; design-based research; digital competency; distance
   education; post-secondary studies; user experience
ID USER EXPERIENCE
AB Introduction Adult students enrolled in asynchronous distance education programs can face challenges using digital technology. To make it easier for adult students to access digital competency development resources, we conducted a study to design, implement, assess and improve a tool called the Digital Compass (Rep & egrave;re num & eacute;rique), which centralizes all available digital technology support resources.Methods The study used a design-based research approach and was conducted in three evaluation and improvement cycles. Data were collected using a netnography to analyze the behaviour of 306 users and a barometer survey administered to 48 participants assessing user experience and satisfaction with resources.Results Results show the tool has a high rate of enrolment. Our analysis shows that nearly two thirds of all actions in the Digital Compass took place outside of working hours and that use of the tool tracks closely with assessment deadlines. The tool was deemed largely positive in terms of practicality, with the descriptors "supportive" and "efficient" obtaining the highest scores. Students were also satisfied with the resources, with 97.3% of students finding them to be useful and relevant.Discussion These findings are a reminder that adults enrolled in distance education are juggling multiple priorities and prove that there is a need for tailored support, specifically by drawing on universal design for learning. These data made it possible to further develop the Digital Compass in order to improve the institutional support provided. The joint use of a netnography and barometer surveys proved to be a suitable data collection methodology for an iterative study of user experience.

TI Evaluating a generative AI-based pitch simulation tool: a pilot study in
   entrepreneurial training
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; entrepreneurial competencies; entrepreneurship
   education; experiential learning; pitch training
ID INVESTORS; IMPACT; INFORMATION
AB Purpose Entrepreneurship education faces persistent challenges in providing scalable, standardized, and feedback-rich training for investor pitch skills. This pilot study developed and evaluated a generative AI-powered pitch simulator designed to replicate investor interactions in a low-pressure training environment.Design A mixed-methods feasibility evaluation was conducted with 46 entrepreneurs. The study integrated post-session quantitative measures of perceived utility and learning value, qualitative thematic analysis of open-ended responses, and behavioral engagement data (interaction duration and message frequency).Findings Participants reported moderate perceived learning value (M = 6.02, SD = 2.30) and helpfulness (M = 6.39, SD = 2.14), with moderate-to-positive willingness to recommend the tool (M = 7.00, SD = 2.53). Qualitative analysis identified the simulator's value as a repeatable, structured practice environment, while a subset of participants also noted reduced emotional and nonverbal fidelity compared to face-to-face investor meetings.Practical implications The simulator functions as a scalable supplementary tool for entrepreneurship education, enabling iterative practice in a standardized setting. The findings also suggest that combining simulator practice with human mentorship may be particularly valuable for addressing interpersonal dimensions of pitch performance.Originality This study contributes an initial empirical evaluation of a generative AI pitch simulator and offers preliminary observations on how such tools might support experiential learning approaches in entrepreneurship education, providing a basis for more rigorous future investigation.

TI Results by macrozone in the national diagnostic assessment: a
   territorial analysis of standards in physical education teacher
   education in Chile
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Chile; initial teacher training; national diagnostic assessment;
   physical education teacher education; territorial inequality
ID INEQUALITIES
AB The Physical Education teacher plays a strategic role within the Chilean educational system, with Initial Teacher Education being a fundamental stage in which professional standards guide their preparation. Within this framework, the National Diagnostic Assessment (NDA) provides nationwide evidence regarding the level of achievement of these standards at the end of the training process. The aim of this study was to analyze and compare the results of Physical Education teacher education students in the 2024 NDA according to the macrozone where their universities are located. A quantitative, cross-sectional, and comparative design was employed, based on official open-access data from the Chilean Ministry of Education (n = 1,098). Descriptive analyses and non-parametric inferential tests (Mann-Whitney U) were conducted. The results reveal a differentiated territorial pattern: the Metropolitan Region and the North-Central Macrozone generally obtain higher averages, whereas the Southern and Northern Macrozones show relatively lower performance. However, effect sizes were predominantly small to moderate, suggesting relative convergence within a standardized national system.

TI Developing sustainability competencies through dual mentorship: a
   qualitative multiple-case study of urban and rural planning education in
   China
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE competencies for sustainable development; dual-mentorship; higher
   education; place-based education; planning education; university
   education for sustainable development; university-community
   collaboration
ID KEY COMPETENCES; INTEGRATION
AB Introduction Higher education is under growing pressure to produce graduates capable of addressing sustainability challenges, yet the gap between classroom theory and real-world practice remains difficult to bridge. This study examines a dual-mentorship model that pairs academic faculty with rural village practitioners as a way to develop sustainability competencies in urban and rural planning education at the undergraduate level in China, focusing on systems thinking, normative competence, and strategic competence. It explores both what the approach achieves and the constraints it faces.Methods The study draws on the "100 Youths Interview 100 Village Secretaries" initiative, a university-wide experiential learning programme. We conducted a qualitative multiple-case study of 10 purposively selected villages, collecting data from reflection journals written by 30 undergraduate students and semi-structured interviews with 10 village party secretaries. A post-fieldwork self-assessment survey provided a descriptive supplement. Data were analysed using a hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis, with the three competency dimensions serving as the initial analytical framework.Results The qualitative evidence shows that pairing field immersion with academic and practitioner mentorship is associated with perceived gains across all three target competency domains. A supplementary post-fieldwork survey corroborates these patterns, with the large majority of students rating the initiative as useful across all domains. Analysis of journals and interviews reveals how these gains arise: students developed systems thinking by tracing the connections among ecological, livelihood, and policy dimensions; strengthened normative competence by working through the value trade-offs embedded in real governance decisions; and built strategic competence through direct exposure to stakeholder negotiation and adaptive implementation in village settings.Discussion The study surfaces persistent challenges around curriculum integration, mentor preparation, and competency assessment, alongside concrete opportunities for practice-embedded and interdisciplinary learning. The findings offer a model for training planning graduates who can translate sustainability principles into action within local governance contexts.

TI Comparison of grades by assessment modality in an Ecuadorian public
   university during the pandemic transition (2019-2020)
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic integrity; academic performance; COVID-19; Latin America;
   PLS-SEM; public university; summative assessment; virtual education
AB The COVID-19 pandemic produced an abrupt transition from in-person to virtual teaching in Latin American public universities, with effects on the comparative validity of summative assessments that remain insufficiently documented. The present study examines whether the average grades obtained by undergraduate students at an Ecuadorian public university differ systematically between the 100% in-person modality (2019) and the 100% virtual modality (2020), and explores the institutional mechanisms that may have produced such differences. A non-experimental, cross-sectional convergent mixed-methods design was adopted, drawing on two complementary sources of evidence: (i) a census sample of more than 19,000 academic records corresponding to three evaluative instances (first partial, second partial, and recovery examinations); and (ii) a structured survey administered to 35 instructors who supervised assessment processes during the virtual period. The quantitative analysis included descriptive statistics, the Welch t-test, the Welch ANOVA with Games-Howell post-hoc correction, and non-parametric robustness tests (Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis). The perceptual component was modeled by means of Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with bootstrap (500 replications). The results show grades that are significantly higher and less dispersed in the virtual modality (Cohen's d between -0.53 and -0.69; p < 0.001 in all instances), a pattern corroborated by the non-parametric tests. The structural model identifies an associative pattern consistent with full mediation: digital gaps are associated with the weakening of evaluative-control mechanisms (beta = 0.658, p < 0.001), and this weakening predicts perceived grade inflation (beta = 0.878, p < 0.001), with a significant indirect effect [beta = 0.578; 95% CI (0.545, 1.306)]. The convergence between census-based evidence and perceptual evidence suggests that the increase observed in the virtual modality may reflect, at least in part, the erosion of institutional control mechanisms during the health emergency rather than an intrinsic improvement in learning. The direct comparison between both modalities therefore demands interpretive caution, in view of the confound between modality and instrument format and of the absence of sociodemographic control variables. These findings have implications for the validity of academic-quality indicators, for the design of post-pandemic hybrid assessment models, and for quality-assurance policies in Latin American higher education.

TI Pre-service science teachers' adaptive pedagogical reasoning in
   AI-supported lesson plans: a case with chemical equilibrium
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE adaptive pedagogical reasoning; artificial intelligence; ChatGPT;
   rationale for lesson design; RCM of PCK
ID STUDENT-TEACHERS; KNOWLEDGE
AB Although generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into lesson planning in teacher education, little is known about how pre-service science teachers adapt AI-generated content through pedagogical reasoning for contextually responsive science teaching. This study explored how AI influences pre-service science teachers' (PSSTs) adaptive pedagogical reasoning (APR) when planning lessons on chemical equilibrium in resource-constrained contexts. Drawing on the Refined Consensus Model of Pedagogical Content Knowledge, APR was conceptualised across four dimensions: identification and anticipation of students' thinking, adaptivity in lesson design, justification of instructional decisions, and alignment with learning goals and differentiation. An exploratory mixed-methods case study was conducted with 19 third-year PSSTs in a South African university. Participants developed traditional and AI-supported lesson plans using the Rationale for Lesson Design framework. Data were analysed using an APR rubric and Rasch analysis. Findings showed that AI-supported planning enhanced anticipation of students' thinking, justification of instructional decisions, and alignment with learning goals and differentiation. However, adaptivity in lesson design remained limited. The study suggests that while AI can scaffold deeper pedagogical reasoning, teacher education programmes should explicitly support adaptive instructional decision-making.

TI Digital transformation in school for mobile learning: insights from
   preservice teachers during the COVID-19 pandemic
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE COVID-19; digital transformation; ICT; mobile learning; PESTLE; TPACK
ID EDUCATION
AB This study investigated challenges in school digital transformation for mobile learning. TI From modelling to scientific creativity: enhancing gifted students'
   scientific creativity in mathematics through modelling-centred
   project-based learning with rotational roles
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE gifted students; inquiry-based learning; mathematical modelling;
   mathematics education; project-based learning; rotational roles;
   scientific creativity; stem education
AB This study examines the effects of modelling-centred project-based learning with rotational roles on students' scientific creativity and inquiry-oriented thinking in mathematics. While modelling and project-based approaches are widely used in STEM education, their effectiveness remains inconsistent, partly due to the lack of structured mechanisms that guide students' engagement in complex cognitive processes. To address this gap, the study proposes an integrated instructional approach that combines modelling-centred learning with rotational role-based collaboration. A quasi-experimental pre-test-post-test control group design was employed with 111 gifted secondary school students in Kazakhstan. The experimental group engaged in modelling-based project work organised through rotating roles (problem poser, model developer, analyst, presenter), while the control group received traditional instruction. In the control group, students studied the same mathematical content within the same instructional timeframe as the experimental group. Instruction was based on a traditional teacher-centred approach, including explanation of concepts, demonstration of procedures, and individual task completion using textbook-based exercises. Students primarily worked on structured problems with predetermined solution methods and did not engage in open-ended modelling tasks, collaborative group work, or role-based activities. The amount of instructional time was comparable across groups, ensuring that differences in learning outcomes could be attributed to the organisation of the learning process rather than differences in content or exposure. The results indicate that the proposed approach enhances students' scientific creativity, with effects varying depending on baseline performance. In contrast, no significant differences were found between groups in inquiry-oriented thinking, although both groups demonstrated improvements over time. Correlation analysis revealed that participation in modelling roles was strongly associated with creativity outcomes, particularly for the problem poser role, while associations with inquiry skills were weak and less consistent. These findings suggest that structured participation within the modelling cycle plays a critical role in fostering scientific creativity, but may be insufficient on its own to support the development of inquiry-oriented thinking. The study contributes to STEM education research by highlighting the importance of pedagogical mechanisms that organise students' engagement in modelling processes and by proposing rotational roles as a practical strategy for structuring collaborative learning.

LA English
DT Article
DE digital literacy; higher education; privacy concerns; technology

ID INFORMATION-TECHNOLOGY; ACCEPTANCE
AB The trend of next-generation digital technologies being more widely used in higher education implies that it is time to deal with the factors that affect their adoption and usage more effectively. The current research normalizes the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) model by the acceptance of digital literacy and privacy concerns and thereby examining the user's engagement, satisfaction, and performance in learning. Despite extensive use of the UTAUT2 framework in higher education, limited research integrates digital literacy and privacy concerns as core determinants of next-generation technology adoption. This study addresses the lack of a comprehensive model examining how these factors interact with traditional predictors to influence behavioral intention and learning outcomes. The results are a validation of the extended UTAUT2 model's robustness and explanatory power. In conclusion, this research has made a significant contribution around technology acceptance by revealing the fact that the successful adoption of modern educational technologies is not only dependent on the perceived usefulness but also on the level of users' digital skills, institutional support, and trust-related factors.

TI Exploratory Factor Analysis of Decision-Making Domains Influencing
   Students' Pursuit of the PharmD Degree at 2 Canadian Universities
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pharmacy education; Academic decision-making; Survey development
ID COLLEGE; CAREER; MOTIVATIONS; ENROLLMENT; RETENTION; EDUCATION; CHOICE;
   SCHOOL
AB Objective: To identify and validate decision-making domains that influence pharmacy students' choice to pursue a Doctor of Pharmacy (PharmD) degree. Methods: A modified questionnaire, adapted from previous research in academic decision-making, was developed and validated for pharmacy students. The instrument included 38 Likert-type items across 5 initial domains. Content and face validity were established through expert and student review. A convenience sample of 170 PharmD students and graduates from 2 Atlantic Canadian universities completed the survey. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize item responses. Exploratory factor analysis using principal component analysis with varimax rotation was conducted to identify underlying domain structures. Reliability was assessed using Cronbach's alpha. Results: The exploratory factor analysis supported a 6-factor model comprising institutional, family, experiential, personal, economic, and career domains. The final model retained 28 items. Cronbach's alpha values ranged from 0.65 to 0.83 across domains, with an overall reliability of 0.83. The model explained 57.32% of the variance in student responses. Conclusion: This research generated a validated and reliable questionnaire aimed at identifying decision-making domains that influence pharmacy students' academic choices. The 6-domain decision-making model offers insights into the multifaceted factors shaping student decisions and provides policy-relevant data useful in understanding student motivations and program expectations, developing targeted recruitment strategies, improving student advising, and informing program development in pharmacy education.

TI Medication disposal knowledge, attitude and practice among
   undergraduates: Implications for pharmacy education
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Medication; Disposal; Knowledge; Attitude; Practice; Undergraduate
ID PHARMACEUTICALS
AB Background: Improper disposal of unused and expired medications contributes to environmental contamination and public health risks. Despite awareness efforts, disposal practices remain inconsistent and public education limited. Undergraduate students represent a key population for shaping long-term behaviors and understanding their knowledge, attitude and practice can inform educational strategies relevant to pharmacy education and public health. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted using a content-validated questionnaire via Microsoft Forms. A pilot study (n = 39) preceded the main survey (n = 108) among undergraduates from diverse disciplines. Data were analyzed using Chi-square/Fisher's exact tests and Spearman's correlation coefficients in IBM SPSS Statistics. Results: Household waste was the most common disposal method (67.6%) and 56.5% had never used a community pharmacy for safe medication disposal. Higher knowledge scores correlated with confidence in advising others (r = -0.412, p < 0.001) and frequent use of community pharmacies (r = 0.213, p = 0.027). Higher attitude scores correlated with confidence (r = -0.356, p < 0.001) but not disposal frequency (r = 0.090, p = 0.354). Knowledge and attitude scores were positively correlated (r = 0.391, p < 0.001). Knowledge level was associated with academic program, prior disposal education and curriculum content; attitude level with academic program and curriculum content only. Conclusion: Undergraduates demonstrate inconsistent medication disposal practices and variable confidence, influenced by knowledge levels and educational exposure. These findings highlight opportunities for pharmacy education to address gaps in medication disposal knowledge and patient counselling skills. A structured, longitudinal pharmacy curriculum, progressing from foundational awareness to applied practice, patient education and community engagement may prepare future pharmacists to promote safe and sustainable medication disposal behaviors.

AB This study investigated the effects of four instructional sequences-Problem Solving Only (PS), Problem Solving-Worked Examples (PS-WE), Worked Examples-Problem Solving (WE-PS), and Worked Examples Only (WE)-on learning performance, cognitive load, mental effort, and judgments of learning (JOLs). TI Concept gesture and concept definition in mathematics with particular
   reference to sequences and limits
SO JOURNAL OF MATHEMATICAL BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE Concept gesture; Concept image; Concept definition; Gestures;
   Embodiment; Real analysis; Sequence; Limit
ID IMAGES
AB Concept image and concept definition, among the most utilised constructs in mathematics education research, emerged in a period characterised by cognitive theories of learning aimed at explaining individual students' mathematical constructions. Acknowledging learning theories that have since developed, and in particular those that emphasise the bodily dimensions of mathematical thinking, in this article we propose concept gesture as a construct that foregrounds the role of the body in mathematical teaching and learning, while expanding on the notions of concept image and concept definition. We illustrate the construct by examining some of a lecturer's mathematical gestures in a first-year university analysis lecture, focusing specifically on those that convey conceptual meaning in relation to the concepts of sequence and limit. We discuss how concept gestures, understood within an embodied perspective, can productively enrich the concept image/definition framework, and suggest practical, theoretical, empirical, and methodological implications.

TI A Qualitative Study Exploring Diabetes Prevention Intervention Needs and
   Ideas Among Young Adults at High Risk for Diabetes
SO JOURNAL OF NUTRITION EDUCATION AND BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE young adult; prediabetes; diabetes prevention; tailored intervention
ID EMERGING ADULTS; OBESITY; OVERWEIGHT; DISPARITIES; OUTCOMES; PROGRAM
AB Objective: To explore perspectives of young adults with prediabetes and high burden of social needs about their intervention needs and ideas for solutions to enable behavior change. Design: Qualitative study with semistructured interviews. Setting: One safety-net hospital and 1 academic medical center in a US city. Participants: Twenty-four publicly-insured adults aged 18-26 years with prediabetes (63% female, 71% Latino/a/x, 29% Black, 61% food insecure, and 39% any college; mean age 22.6 years). Phenomenon of Interest and Variables: Internal and external factors affecting dietary and exercise behaviors, within the Capability-Opportunity-Motivation-Behavior framework. Analysis: Data were analyzed using a general inductive approach followed by directed content analysis within the Capability-Opportunity-Motivation-Behavior framework. Results: Participants reported few intervention needs regarding Capability, with sophisticated nutrition knowledge and an accurate understanding of prediabetes. Major Opportunity needs emerged, including the high cost of food not offset by the food safety net, internalized effects of immersion in unhealthy environments, and low control over time. Motivation varied: most desired to avoid diabetes, but interviewees had mixed perceptions of their risk and self-efficacy. Interviewees shared 23 Intervention Ideas to address identified needs. Conclusions: Our findings can inform youth-centered multimodal diabetes prevention interventions for young adults at high risk of diabetes that leverage existing knowledge, address Opportunity barriers, and differentiate among subgroups with varying motivation.

TI Examining the Invariance of a Common Household Food Insecurity Measure
   Across Various Adult and Child Characteristics
SO JOURNAL OF NUTRITION EDUCATION AND BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE food security; measurement invariance; sex; race; ethnicity
ID GENDER-DIFFERENCES; UNITED-STATES; SECURITY; HEALTH; DISPARITIES;
   EXPERIENCE; ACCESS; DIET
AB Objective: To examine whether the 10-item Household Food Security Survey Module (HFSSM) measure validly captures experiences of food insecurity between and across certain groups. Design: Cross-sectional study. Participants: The 2019 National Health Interview Survey child survey (n = 1,575). Main Outcome Measure: Household Food Security Survey Module experience among respondent characteristics, including child sex, racial and ethnic groups, adult sex, and relative status. Analysis: Confirmatory factor analysis was conducted to explore the construct validity of the HFSSM and was used as a baseline model for invariance testing. Invariance testing proceeded using multiple group confirmatory factor analysis, which included configural and scalar invariance because of the binary nature of the data. Results: Confirmatory factor analysis results indicate that a 1-factor model was the best fit for the data. The HFSSM was invariant within the child sex, racial, and ethnic groups, and relative status variables, but the adult sex variable was found to be noninvariant. Conclusions and Implications: The HFSSM can be used for cross-group comparisons in invariant variables. However, female and male adults reporting on behalf of children appear to interpret the measure differently. These data support the use of additional modeling procedures to account for the noninvariance between adult sexual identity when using the HFSSM.

TI More PEAS Please! Implementation Methodology of a
   Preschool Program Promoting Healthy Eating, Science, and Language
SO JOURNAL OF NUTRITION EDUCATION AND BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE Head Start; preschool; STEAM; fruit and vegetable consumption;
   food-based learning
ID HEAD-START TEACHERS; FOOD-BASED SCIENCE; NUTRITION EDUCATION; CLASSROOM;
   INSTRUCTION; PREFERENCES; TECHNOLOGY; KNOWLEDGE; CHILDREN; SKILLS
AB Objective: Preschool Education in Applied Sciences (PEAS) intervention, a multicomponent intervention designed to improve teachers' science teaching self-efficacy and enhance children's fruit and vegetable consumption, science knowledge, and language development. Design: A 2-group (comparison/delayed intervention) quasi-experimental design was employed. Teachers completed baseline, formative, and postintervention surveys. Intervention teachers also completed a postintervention interview. Child outcomes were assessed at 3 timepoints (baseline, preintervention, and postintervention) using validated measures. Setting: Thirteen Head Start centers in central North Carolina. Participants: Ninety-four teachers (n = 44 intervention; n = 50 comparison) and 330 English-speaking children aged 3-5 years (n = 140 intervention; n = 190 comparison), based on power analysis estimates. Intervention: Components included a 1-day Kick-Starter Workshop, 6 eLearning modules, PEAS teaching guide featuring 12 classroom activities, and center-based implementation supports including individualized coaching, peer learning communities, and farm to early care and education resources. Main Outcome Measures: Teacher outcomes included self-reported teaching self-efficacy. Child outcomes include fruit and vegetable consumption (skin carotenoids via Veggie Meter (R)), height/weight, science knowledge, and academic vocabulary. Analysis: Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, paired t tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and regression models. Qualitative data were analyzed phenomenologically.

TI On the challenges of investigating lasting learning: A commentary
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Lasting learning; Meaningful learning; Desirable difficulties; Practical
   relevance; Theory development
ID COGNITIVE ARCHITECTURE
AB This commentary discusses the special issue "Toward lasting learning: Cognitive mechanisms and instructional means to maintain the outcomes of meaningful learning". The call for this special issue specified the following prerequisites for the single contributions. First, they should test theoretical assumptions about the conditions and processes of meaningful lasting learning. Second, they should use authentic educational materials. Third, lasting learning should be assessed after a delay of 1 week at minimum. These prerequisites should assure that the contributions have theoretical relevance as well as practical relevance for lasting learning. The seven contributions of this special issue are discussed against this background. Overall, the present special issue can be seen as outstanding in terms of the consistently high quality of the individual contributions in terms of the usual criteria for basic research on learning and instruction. However, although the individual contributions adhere to the specified prerequisites, they have taken merely first steps towards theoretical as well as practical relevance for lasting learning. Possible next steps are proposed to strengthen the theoretical foundation of future studies on meaningful lasting learning (e.g., a more differentiated theoretical conception of lasting learning) as well as to advance their practical relevance (e.g., adopting a multidimensional stance on ecological validity).

TI Learning-in-interaction against stereotypes: How high-achieving girls
   sustain science identities in secondary science
SO LEARNING CULTURE AND SOCIAL INTERACTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Learning-in-interaction; Science identity; Gender stereotypes;
   Recognition; Positioning; Grounded theory
ID GENDER STEREOTYPES; THREAT; ACHIEVEMENT; EXPECTATIONS; EXPERIENCES;
   WOMEN; MODEL
AB Despite decades of policy effort, gendered discourses that frame science as masculine continue to shape girls' access to participation, recognition, and belonging in secondary science classrooms. This study examines how high-achieving girls sustain their participation in and achievement in science while negotiating stereotype pressure through everyday interactions with teachers, peers, and families. Using a socioculturally informed Straussian grounded theory design, we analysed indepth interviews with 20 high-performing female science-track students from a key public high school in G City, China. Analysis centered on narrated episodes of classroom talk, assessment feedback, parental messaging, and peer positioning. Through open, axial, and selective coding, we developed an interaction-centered process model with three linked components: (1) identity repositioning and cognitive schema reconstruction, (2) emotionally scaffolded resilience across family, school, and peer contexts, and (3) volitional control that stabilizes effort and reframes stereotype-related threat into task value and strategic participation. Findings show that recognition is distributed across settings: supportive school feedback and equitable participation opportunities, together with parental affirmation and counter-stereotypical role-model narratives, help girls maintain legitimacy as science learners and sustain high performance. Implications are discussed for recognition-oriented pedagogy, teacher professional development on implicit bias, and cross-context supports that sustain girls' STEM trajectories.

TI "Teaching without time to think": An interpretive qualitative study of
   academic identity, moral distress, and sustainability in the nurse
   educator workforce☆
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nurse educators; Academic identity; Moral distress; Educator workforce;
   Workforce sustainability; Nursing education reform
ID JOB-SATISFACTION; STUDENTS
AB Background: Nursing and midwifery education is being reshaped by rapid higher education and health system reforms that prioritise teaching delivery, accountability, and performance reporting. While educator workforce concerns are often framed ar workload and capacity problems, less is known about how reform pressures disrupt nurse educators academic identity and moral integrity, with implications for long-term workforce sustainability.<br /> Aim: To explore how reform-related pressures influence academic identity, experiences of moral distress, and perceptions of sustainability among nurse educators.<br /> Design: Interpretive qualitative study.<br /> Settingz A public University nursing education context within a rapidly reforming health and higher education system.<br /> Participantz: Nurse educators (pi = 15) purposively sampled to reflect variation in academic role and experience.<br /> Methods: Semi-structured interviews were conducted, audio-recorded, and transcribed verbatim. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Strategies to enhance trustworthiness included reflexive journaling, team discussion of theme development, and an audit trail.<br /> Results: Three interconnected themes were identified. Moral distress and compromised values captured ethical tension and emotional burden when educators felt constrained from providing the quality of teaching, arness-ment, and student support they considered professionally necessary. From scholar to service provider described erosion of academik identity under intensified teaching and administrative demands, reduced scholarly time, and diminished autonomy. Sustainability under strain reflected questioning of long-term academic careers, reduced mentoring capacity, and concerns about the future nurse educator workforce. Participants repeatedly charac-terised their work as "teaching without time to think."<br /> Conclusions: Reform-related pressures threaten nurse educator sustainability not only through workload but through identity duruption and moral distress. Workforce strategies should protect time for scholarly engage-ment, strengthen mentoring infrastructures, and create organisational conditions that support ethical teaching practice to sustain nursing education quality under reform.

TI Parental-adolescent educational expectation congruence and positive
   mental health: A response surface analysis for the mediating role of
   psychological capital
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Adolescents' own educational expectations (AOEE); Perceived parental
   educational expectations (PPEE); Positive mental health (PMH);
   Psychological capital (PsyCap); Response surface analysis (RSA)
ID DISCREPANCIES; PERFORMANCE; IMPACT
AB Adolescents' positive mental health plays a critical role in their developmental trajectories, and the alignment or discrepancy between parental and adolescent educational expectations represents an important yet underexamined relational context within family education. The present study investigates the association between perceived parent-adolescent educational expectation congruence and adolescents' positive mental health, while further examining the mediating role of psychological capital. Using survey data from 3023 Chinese adolescents, polynomial regression and response surface analysis were employed to capture the association patterns of congruence and incongruence between perceived parental educational expectations and adolescents' own educational expectations, including both their direction and magnitude, were associated with positive mental health and psychological capital. The findings indicate that greater congruence, particularly at higher levels, is associated with higher levels of both positive mental health and psychological capital. In contrast, incongruence is associated with lower levels of these outcomes, with more pronounced negative associations observed when perceived parental expectations exceed adolescents' own expectations and as the discrepancy increases. Further analyses reveal that psychological capital serves as a significant mediating mechanism linking perceived expectation congruence to positive mental health. By adopting a congruence-based perspective, this study extends current understanding of the developmental mechanisms underlying adolescent positive mental health and highlights the importance of fostering coordinated parent-adolescent communication around educational goals, as well as promoting adolescents' psychological capital in family and school-based interventions.

TI Exploring undergraduate students' synthesis writing strategies and
   perceptions in a GenAI-supported literature review task
SO JOURNAL OF ENGLISH FOR ACADEMIC PURPOSES
LA English
DT Article
DE GenAI writing assistance tools; Self-reported strategies; Synthesis
   writing strategies
AB Educators recognize that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can change the way students write and think about writing. However, there are concerns that overreliance on GenAI tools will result in a decrease in the cognitive effort needed to write. This study sought to examine the synthesis writing strategies used by undergraduate students during a literature review task supported by a specialized GenAI tool. The literature review is commonly described as a challenging synthesis task that involves complex cognitive processes. Participants were provided with a literature review task and given access to the GenAI tool. They completed a self-reported strategy use survey and written reflections, followed by a stimulated recall protocol and an interview to provide further evidence of their synthesis writing strategies. Findings showed frequent use of skimming, reading summaries, evaluating sources, and drawing connections among sources, reflecting the strategies students employed to select, organize, and connect information when using the GenAI tool. While the focus on connecting and organizing strategies suggests that they are attempting to critically evaluate the GenAI output, reliance on the provided summaries may indicate a lack of critical engagement with the sources. These complexities underscore the need for educators to ensure that students remain actively engaged in selecting, organizing, and connecting sources when GenAI tools are involved.

TI Experiences of caregivers of autistic children in urban South India:
   Insights from caregivers and providers
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism; Caregiver; Stigma; Coping
ID SPECTRUM DISORDER; PARENTS PERSPECTIVES; EARLY INTERVENTION; AFFILIATE
   STIGMA; IMPACT; MOTHERS; STRESS; DISABILITIES; DIAGNOSIS
AB Caregivers of autistic children in resource-limited countries such as India face multifaceted challenges. Research on culturally specific experiences of caregivers navigating their child's autism diagnosis is limited and hinders effective partnership and alliance with caregivers. This study explored the experiences of caregivers of autistic children in Bengaluru, South India. Indepth, semi-structured interviews were conducted with twenty caregivers of autistic children and eight providers, including educators and early-intervention providers. Transcripts were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis. Five themes describe caregivers' complex journeys of receiving, navigating, and coping with their child's autism diagnosis. Parental and healthcare provider awareness regarding autism is limited, leading to widespread normalization of developmental delays. Second, caregivers experience a high burden of care and prominent stigma regarding autism, which affect their interpersonal, psychological, and financial well-being. Third, beliefs on the etiology of autism vary and inform how caregivers approach solutions and therapies. Finally, caregivers use various coping strategies to navigate stigma and accept their child's diagnosis. These findings highlight the need for culturally adapted interventions that support caregiver well-being and coping and empower caregivers as pivotal stakeholders in their child's development.

TI Making chemistry labs more relevant - development and evaluation of
   contextualised pre-lab materials for qualitative inorganic analysis
SO CHEMISTRY TEACHER INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE context-based learning; design-based research; Eurovariety 2025;
   inorganic chemistry; lab education; first-year undergraduate
ID UNIVERSAL DESIGN; IM-KONTEXT; STUDENT; MEANINGFUL; SCIENCE;
   LABORATORIES; FRAMEWORK; EDUCATION; GOALS
AB In undergraduate chemistry lab courses it is common to jointly teach students with different academic backgrounds, previous experiences, interests and career aspirations. A neglect of this diversity can lead to missing relevance of the learning content, frustration, and higher drop-out rates. Although the perceived relevance can significantly impact students' learning outcomes, this potential has been largely overlooked. Context-based learning offers great potential to increase students' perceived relevance by connecting the learning content to real-world contexts. However, there is a lack of suitable learning materials so far. We present a design-based research study consisting of 3 iterations giving insights into the development and evaluation process of contextualised pre-lab learning materials to increase the perceived relevance of a first-year undergraduate qualitative inorganic lab course. The materials contain battery recycling as real-world context, professional references to school and chemistry industry, chemical inquiry methods, and scientific reasoning skills. For the evaluation we involved different stakeholders and applied a mixed-methods methodology incorporating semi-structured think-aloud interviews and an online questionnaire. The results confirm a high potential of the materials. Besides our final materials, we provide implications for the design of contextualised pre-lab learning materials that make university chemistry labs more relevant for students with diverse backgrounds.

TI Modelling strategic patterns in high school students' mathematical
   problem solving: an AI-based approach integrating simulated data and
   clustered process analysis
SO LEARNING FUTURES AND EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Modelling; Problem solving; Quantitative
   reasoning; Problem solving process
AB Purpose This study investigates how students approach number-pattern problems in mathematics and whether their problem-solving strategies can be meaningfully clustered using artificial intelligence (AI) techniques. It aims to identify latent strategy profiles (e.g. guess-and-check, efficient solving, help-seeking) from digital process data to support more personalized and adaptive instruction.Design/methodology/approach This study generated synthetic student data simulating distinct strategy types and validated clustering algorithms on it. Hence, it applied the same clustering techniques to real-world student log data from ASSISTments, using features such as attempt count, hint usage and time per problem. The study evaluated cluster quality using Silhouette and Adjusted Rand Index scores and interpreted clusters through comparisons with simulated strategy types.Findings Five distinct student strategy profiles emerged in both simulated and real datasets. Core patterns, including efficient solvers, guessers and help-seeker, were consistently identified. Some real-data clusters aligned with the simulated types, while others revealed new, plausible strategies not captured in the initial models. This validates the clustering approach and highlights the complexity of real student behaviour.Research limitations/implications The real-world data used had limited behavioural features (e.g. no information about diagram use or off-platform reasoning), potentially obscuring subtler strategies. Some clusters may represent blended or transitional strategies. Further studies using richer log data and triangulation (e.g. interviews, screen recordings) could improve interpretability.Practical implications Cluster awareness serves as formative assessment and enables differentiation: (i) rapid guessers - require rule articulation and self-monitoring; (ii) efficient/explicit solvers - offer extensions to deepen generalization; (iii) misconception-prone (e.g. linear projection on exponential) - prioritize early remediation; (iv) hint-forward - coach strategic help-seeking, not suppress it (Dalmaijer et al., 2022; Steinley, 2006). For learning analytics/ITS, surface interpretable indicators (error trajectories, hint sequences, pacing) and deliver profile-contingent prompts in real time (e.g. "state the rule before the next attempt", "try a smaller step and check the rule"), with human-in-the-loop oversight and no punitive tracking (Lim, 2024). Operationally: denoise outlier dwell times, report k-selection stability, triangulate algorithms and add sequence-aware features.Social implications For adoption, strategy profiling must centre transparency, equity and teacher empowerment. Dashboards/tutors should show which behavioural signals drive profiles, display confidence/uncertainty and prohibit punitive uses (e.g. tracking/labels without support). Institutions should monitor subgroup disparities in cluster assignment and outcomes, pair profiles with supportive - not exclusionary - interventions, and enforce privacy/consent for log data. Prioritize professional learning so educators interpret clusters responsibly and integrate them into formative practice. Such governance aligns AI-enabled analytics with instructional judgement and public trust (Pedro et al., 2019; Guan et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2023; Wagner, 2022).Originality/value This study combines simulation and real-data clustering to reveal latent student strategies, demonstrating how AI methods can complement educational theory.
   It highlights that even with coarse log features, unsupervised learning can uncover interpretable behavioural patterns. The findings contribute to advancing data-driven personalized education.

TI Experiences of international students using artificial intelligence
   (AI): tools for cultural adaptation, academic success and self-directed
   learning
SO LEARNING FUTURES AND EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence in education; International students; Academic
   adaptation; Self-directed learning; Intercultural education
AB Purpose This study explores how international students from the Western Balkans use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to support academic adaptation, writing development and self-directed learning in Anglophone higher education institutions. By examining their lived experiences through qualitative interviews, this research aims to understand AI's role as both a cognitive scaffold and a transformational partner in learning. This study also addresses equity, ethics and overreliance, contributing theoretical insights and practical implications for inclusive, AI-enhanced education.Design/methodology/approach The study used a qualitative research design within a constructivist-interpretivist paradigm to explore international students' experiences with AI. Nine undergraduate students from Kosovo, Albania and North Macedonia studying at UK and US institutions were recruited through purposive sampling. Data were collected in three phases: orientation, semi-structured interviews in Albanian and member checking. Interviews were transcribed, translated and analyzed using Braun and Clarke's (2006) six-phase thematic analysis. Intercoder agreement, reflexive journaling and an audit trail enhanced rigor. Ethical standards were followed in line with the Declaration of Helsinki and APA guidelines.Findings AI tools supported international students' adaptation by simplifying complex texts, clarifying assignments and reducing language-related anxiety. Participants described AI as a "silent tutor," enhancing comprehension, academic writing and confidence. Beyond correction, AI fostered self-directed learning by enabling students to plan, summarize and test understanding independently. However, concerns emerged around unequal access to premium tools, ethical boundaries and potential overreliance, which risk undermining critical thinking and autonomy. Overall, AI was experienced as both a scaffold for inclusion and a challenge requiring institutional guidance to ensure equitable and responsible use in higher education.Research limitations/implications The study's small, purposive sample of nine students from the Western Balkans limits generalizability and may not capture the full diversity of international learners. Reliance on self-reported experiences also introduces subjectivity. Despite these constraints, the findings provide valuable insights into an underexplored population in AI-in-education research. Future studies should use larger, comparative and longitudinal designs to examine evolving patterns of AI use across contexts. Expanding beyond Western Balkan students will further validate and extend these findings, helping to shape inclusive, ethical and evidence-based policies for AI integration in higher education.Practical implications The findings highlight the need for universities to integrate AI literacy into academic skills programs, enabling students to use tools ethically and effectively. Faculty can leverage AI to scaffold writing, comprehension and independent learning while modeling responsible practices. Institutions should provide equitable access to premium AI platforms to reduce disparities among students from different economic backgrounds. Clear policies and support structures are essential to balance innovation with integrity, ensuring AI use enhances, rather than undermines, autonomy and critical thinking. Such measures can foster inclusive, AI-enhanced learning environments that better support international students.
   Social implications This study underscores how AI can reduce barriers for culturally and linguistically diverse learners, supporting inclusion and academic success in global higher education. At the same time, unequal access to premium AI tools risks reinforcing social and digital divides, particularly for students from less-resourced regions. Establishing equitable access and ethical frameworks is therefore critical to ensure AI empowers rather than marginalizes learners. By addressing these issues, universities and policymakers can promote fairness, strengthen international student integration and foster a more inclusive, technologically supported society where AI contributes to educational opportunity and social mobility.Originality/value To the best of the authors' knowledge, this study is one of the first to explore how international students from the Western Balkans engage with AI to support academic adaptation, writing and self-directed learning in Anglophone higher education. By focusing on an underrepresented student population, it offers fresh insights into the cultural and linguistic dimensions of AI use, beyond commonly studied Global North and Asian contexts. The integration of transformational learning (Mezirow, 1997) and self-directed learning (Knowles, 1975) theories provides a novel interpretive lens, extending their application into digital, AI-mediated environments and contributing both theoretical depth and practical guidance for inclusive AI adoption.

TI A Precollege Summer Enrichment Chemistry Workshop and Its Impact on
   Student Progression and Success
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Incoming College Students; Academic Preparedness; Confidence; Mindset;
   Belonging
ID GENERAL-CHEMISTRY; UNDERGRADUATE STEM; PREPARATORY COURSE; BRIDGING
   COURSE; IMPLEMENTATION; PERFORMANCE; PROGRAM; PERSISTENCE; TRANSITION;
   UNIVERSITY
AB We describe the Summer Enrichment Chemistry Workshop (SECW), a unique program in its dual role as both a bridge and a revised placement program. The SECW is a tuition-free, six-week summer program designed for first-time college students who have received a preparatory placement in chemistry. This course offers an opportunity for performance-based revised placement. Students who successfully complete the workshop may take General Chemistry 1 or Comprehensive General and Organic Chemistry. The workshop is held at an urban R1 research university in the Midwest, which has strong affiliations with a hospital and a health sciences system. The workshop focuses on foundational skills necessary for success in a first-semester general chemistry course. Emphasis is placed on mastering chemical vocabulary and concepts and applying them with basic math skills to solve diverse problems. In this paper, we examine the workshop's structure and goals, highlighting its distinctive features and impact on student success, including graduation rates, STEM retention, and lower DFW (D-grade, fail, or withdrawal) rates in General Chemistry I. Notably, student interviews revealed unanticipated benefits such as enhanced academic preparedness, confidence, mindset, sense of belonging, and placement outcomes, even in the absence of formal grading.

TI The unity of research and teaching under threat: Does it matter for
   academics' job satisfaction?
SO RESEARCH IN COMPARATIVE AND INTERNATIONAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE higher education; teaching-research nexus; job satisfaction;
   country-comparative research; university stratification
ID WORK; FACULTY; COHERENCE; STRESSORS; EDUCATION; HAPPINESS; SENSE
AB The growing importance of third-party funding, excellence policies, and organisational differentiation are eroding the Humboldtian idea of a unity of research and teaching. Though studies show a perceived preference for research over teaching amongst academics, there remains a dearth of research into the association between the research-teaching nexus and job satisfaction. We know little about whether, and if so how, national higher education contexts moderate job satisfaction. This study examines what effect, if any, the perceived preference for research, the compatibility of research and teaching, and workload have on job satisfaction and whether effects are moderated by country - selecting Canada, Germany, and Austria for comparison. Findings indicate that while high teaching and administrative workloads decrease job satisfaction, those who subjectively prefer teaching over research are more satisfied than their research-oriented colleagues. The results also show that national higher education systems are a significant moderating factor for job satisfaction, highlighting the importance of country-comparative research.

TI Gender and Institutional Differences in Preferred Resident Responses to
   Biased Statements in Medical Education: A Descriptive, Cross-Sectional
   Analysis
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
AB Background: Bias and microaggressions remain persistent challenges in medical education, threatening psychological safety and perpetuating inequities. How learners respond to these incidents and the influence of gender and institutional culture on these responses remain underexplored. Objective: To evaluate preferred strategies for responding to biased statements among emergency medicine residents, comparing differences by gender and institutional affiliation. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, an anonymous survey was distributed to residents at two academic institutions: the University of Utah and UT Southwestern. Participants ranked five possible responses to biased comments originating from patients, staff, peers, and learners. Descriptive statistics and Mann-Whitney U tests were used to analyze differences by gender and institution. Results: Among 100 respondents (52% female), the majority preferred active engagement-either addressing the bias directly or collaborating with an attending-across all scenarios. Ignoring bias was consistently the least preferred option. Gender differences were significant in responses to biased staff statements: men showed a stronger preference for addressing the issue themselves (p = 0.005), while women showed a stronger preference for collaborating with an attending (p = 0.03). Institutional differences were also observed (p < 0.05). UT Southwestern residents more often favoring attending-led/collaborative approaches in patient and staff scenarios, whereas University of Utah residents more often favored addressing bias themselves. Conclusions: Residents generally favored proactive responses to biased statements, with distinct differences based on gender and institutional culture. These findings suggest the need for tailored bias response training that considers both individual and organizational factors. Further research should explore how other identity variables (e.g., race, sexual orientation) intersect with response preferences and how institutions can foster environments that empower all learners to address bias confidently.

TI Teaching difficult Indigenous topics through textual analysis: a
   demonstration of metalogue in secondary English
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Difficult knowledge text; Difficult knowledge guiding practices;
   Indigenous content; Classroom talk; Textual analysis; Dialogue
ID PEDAGOGY; CURRICULUM; KNOWLEDGE; TENSIONS
AB In this paper, we replicate and reflect on the experience of using dialogue to engage with difficult Indigenous topics in a secondary English classroom. Although we are a group of three experienced teachers from diverse familial and professional backgrounds, we take on the role of secondary school English students enacting a metalogue on a difficult Indigenous topic. Specifically, we focus on the pamphlet circulated by the Australian Government to all households in 2023, which provided detailed information about the proposed constitutional changes to establish an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Voice. This pamphlet includes 4000 words of arguments from both the Yes and No camps, each presenting their case for or against the proposed law. Our research addressed two primary questions: (1) What emerges from the textual analysis of "The Pamphlet" when explored through a recursive dialogue? and (2) What practices enable respectful dialogue around the language features of "The Pamphlet" as a difficult knowledge text? Our textual analysis identified key textual features of "The Pamphlet", including use of time as a persuasive device, repetition, and the interplay of logos, pathos, and ethos. Additionally, our cogenerative dialogue and inductive thematic analysis identified four guiding practices for dialoguing around Indigenous matters in English classrooms. These are: situated, dialogic practices; being guided by ethical and emotional sensitivities; being informed by an awareness of positionality and diversity, and commitment to inquiry as generative action.

TI Refugee-background students' biographical perspectives as the enablers
   of praxis in Australia's EAL/D classrooms: a scoping review
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Refugee-background students; EAL/D; Praxis; Australia
ID EDUCATION; SCHOOL; JUSTICE; ENGLISH; ISSUES
AB This scoping review explored refugee-background students' biographical perspectives, including their lived histories, experiences, and linguistic, cultural, and social capital, as enabling praxis in Australia's English as an Additional Language/Dialect EAL/D classrooms. Guided by Arksey and O'Malley's framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, 25 studies (010-2025) were systematically reviewed. Grounded in a praxis-oriented and intra-categorical understanding of diversity, this study conceptualises biographical perspectives (BPs) as relational constructs shaping how refugee-background students (RBS) think, act, and relate within the EAL/D classroom. Analysis revealed four interrelated themes: lived histories and forms of capital, resource mobilisation, visibility, and belonging, showing that BPs operate relationally across these dimensions. The reviewed studies conceptualised RBS' BPs as individual resources for participation and learning. Yet they overlooked their structural and relational dimensions, leaving a conceptual gap between recognising BPs as habitus and theorising it as praxis shaped by power and inequality. Accordingly, these studies lacked the use of a praxis-oriented and intersectional lens that situates BPs as the analytical and transformative core of classroom life. This review, therefore, calls for praxis-oriented research adopting Bourdieu's relational sociology from the analytical lens of intra-categorical intersectionality to reconceptualise BPs as enablers of pedagogical transformation, bridging identity, structure, and inclusion.

TI How Students Use ChatGPT in Biochemistry Education: Evaluating Students'
   Prompts, Illustrations, and Reflective Assessments as Evidence
SO BIOCHEMISTRY AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; ChatGPT; peptide bonding
ID PERFORMANCE
AB The present study aimed to investigate the utilization of ChatGPT by students in the context of learning biochemical concepts. To this end, 25 first-year students enrolled in the Medical Laboratory Techniques program were asked to illustrate a dipeptide composed of alanine and cysteine. The students were instructed to seek guidance exclusively from ChatGPT, without any interaction with the instructor. Subsequently, they were requested to draw on paper the dipeptide structure they believed to be accurate. The prompts submitted to ChatGPT by the students, the responses provided by ChatGPT, and the students' peptide illustrations were systematically examined. In addition, participants were assessed on their experience through a Reflective Evaluation Form. The findings revealed that, rather than engaging with the process to learn how to draw a dipeptide, students predominantly attempted to have ChatGPT generate the drawing for them. The majority of prompts focused on requesting a direct illustration of the peptide. Notably, all structural representations generated by ChatGPT were found to contain errors. Despite possessing the conceptual knowledge required to identify these inaccuracies, the students drew the flawed illustrations on their paper without critical assessment. In their reflective evaluations, students reported that ChatGPT's failure to deliver a definitive molecular structure of dipeptide led to confusion. They expressed the need for a figure of authority to validate the accuracy of the peptide structure, identifying the instructor as the appropriate individual for this role. Furthermore, they conveyed a clear preference for instructor-led guidance over reliance on artificial intelligence in such learning contexts.

TI Bridging spaces towards inclusion: Inclusive pedagogy in
   disability-specific after-school centres (KDAP-AMEA) in Greece
SO BRITISH JOURNAL OF SPECIAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE after-school education; disability-specific provision; inclusive
   education; inclusive pedagogy; KDAP-AMEA
ID EDUCATION; TEACHERS; CHILDREN
AB Centres for Creative Occupation for People with Disabilities (KDAP-AMEA) are disability-specific after-school structures in Greece operating within the broader framework of inclusive education and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD). Grounded in rights-based principles that emphasise participation, agency, and equal access, this qualitative study explores how special educators working in KDAP-AMEA conceptualise and enact inclusive pedagogy, the challenges they encounter, and the structural conditions shaping their practice. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 12 educators across multiple regions and analysed thematically. Findings indicate that educators frame inclusion primarily as meaningful participation, relational belonging, and the cultivation of agency through collaborative and experiential practices. Participants reported enhanced peer interaction, communication, confidence, and socio-emotional development among children. At the same time, structural barriers-including funding instability, employment precarity, limited accessibility, and fragmented professional development-constrain the sustainability of inclusive practices. The study contributes to debates on disability-specific provision by suggesting that KDAP-AMEA may function as bridging spaces within broader inclusive ecosystems, provided that they are embedded in coherent rights-based and policy-supported frameworks.

TI Evolution of learning patterns during the first years at university and
   their relationship with academic stress, effort, and performance
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Learning patterns; Academic stress; Effort; Academic performance; Higher
   education
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; STUDENT; STYLES; PERSPECTIVE; SPANISH
AB This study examines how learning beliefs and strategies-referred to as learning patterns-evolve among Ibero-American students during the first 2 years of university. It also explores the relationship between these patterns, academic stress, and performance. This study aims to shed light on these dynamics (beliefs and learning strategies) to address the persistently high rates of early university dropout in Ibero-America. The participants are 458 students enrolled in Educational Sciences programmes across eight different universities. The Inventory of Learning patterns of Students (ILS) was applied to identify learning patterns (Meaning Directed, Application Directed, Reproduction Directed, and Undirected or the combination between their components). The Academic Stress Questionnaire at University (CEAU) was used to measure stressors, R-CEA for reactions to stress, and A-CEA for coping strategies. Additionally, effort was identified with a Likert scale under the student's perception, and academic performance was calculated based on grade point average. The results highlighted the notable advantages enjoyed by students with high level of self-regulation and academic stress coping strategies. Conversely, students who scored high on external regulation or lack regulation, who lacked effective coping strategies and exhibited certificate-oriented motivation, faced greater challenges in adapting to university and tended to perform less well academically. The study suggested how university teachers can help students with a lack of regulation or external regulation strategies to improve their academic performance and better cope with academic challenges, especially in cases with high levels of academic stress and difficulties in socio-emotional management, among others.

TI Self-efficacy, engagement, learning outcomes, well-being, and overall
   perceived satisfaction in university students
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Student engagement; Learning outcomes; Students' efficacy; Well-being;
   Overall satisfaction; Vietnam
ID SCHOOL; MOTIVATION; MODEL
AB Student engagement is a critical determinant of success in higher education, influencing both academic achievement and personal development. Despite its importance, its conceptualization and measurement vary widely. This study aims to further explore the factor structure of student engagement, arguing for a more convergent approach to engagement in higher education. This study then investigates the relationship among students' self-efficacy, engagement, learning outcomes, well-being, and students' overall satisfaction with the university. Survey data from 371 students at a university in Ho Chi Minh City were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Results confirm engagement as a higher-order, three-factor construct (cognitive, behavioral, and emotional), with behavioral engagement as a second-order construct. Findings reveal that self-efficacy is significantly associated with both engagement (beta = 0.425, p < 0.001) and learning outcomes (beta = 0.551, p < 0.001), with engagement showing an indirect relationship linking self-efficacy to well-being (beta = 0.568, p < 0.001) and to learning outcomes (beta = 0.235, p < 0.001), consistent with full and partial mediation patterns, respectively. Gender moderates the link between learning outcomes and well-being (significant for females only), while academic rank influences the engagement-wellbeing relationship. These findings highlight the interconnectedness of these constructs and their implications for fostering student success. Overall satisfaction correlates positively with self-efficacy, engagement, learning outcomes, and well-being. These results extend engagement theory by clarifying its structure and patterns consistent with mediation roles in the Vietnamese context, offering theoretical and practical insights for fostering student success. We recommend targeted interventions to enhance self-efficacy and engagement, addressing gender-specific needs and academic progression. Methodologically, we recommend the need for longitudinal or experimental designs to properly test mediation of student engagement.

TI Impact of medical student-led surgical simulation curriculum on student
   confidence in the operating room in a limited resource setting
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Medical student education; Surgical simulation; Near-peer teaching;
   Confidence; Low-resource setting
ID PROCEDURAL SKILLS
AB Purpose Although simulation has been widely used to build the skillset of learners, data on how to best implement cost-effective and medical-student-driven simulation programs are lacking. We sought to determine the impact of implementing a surgical skills simulation clerkship course on medical students' confidence going into the operating room. Methods We designed a low-cost surgical simulation clerkship curriculum focused on opening, closing, anatomy, and post-operative care, with a budget under $1000 annually. Over one year, 230 students participated; 117 completed paired pre- and post-session surveys (51.3% response rate). Questionnaires administered pre-session, immediately post-session, and at 3- and 6-month follow-up assessed confidence and perceived benefit on a Likert scale. Wilcoxon signed rank test compared pre- to post-session confidence, Dunnett's test assessed confidence retention, and Spearman's correlation examined associations between surgical interest, OR exposure, and perceived benefit. Results There was significant improvement in pre- to post-session median confidence for: preparation for the OR learning environment, suturing, knot-tying, laparoscopic anatomy, sterile and scrub technique post-operative care, laparoscopy knowledge, identification and handling of surgical instruments, respectful and safe behavior in the operating room, and operating room protocols (all p < 0.05). 92.3% of students found the curriculum beneficial, with benefit positively correlated with surgical interest (r = 0.31, p < 0.05). Conclusions Our curriculum effectively improves and sustains student confidence while minimizing common implementation barriers.

TI Impact of metacognitive interventions on student performance and
   confidence in introductory biology courses
SO JOURNAL OF MICROBIOLOGY & BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE metacognitive intervention; lower-order questions (LOQs); higher-order
   questions (HOQs); confidence level; introductory biology courses
AB This study investigates the impact of a metacognitive intervention on student content performance and confidence across three key biology content modules: protein, respiration, and cell division. The intervention, conducted in Fall 2021 across six large classrooms at three institutions, included two treatment groups and one control group, alternating by module. A two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and post hoc analyses were used to identify group differences. Results show that metacognitive strategies significantly enhanced student performance in the protein module, the first to receive the intervention, with notable score gains in the treatment group. Students with metacognitive training performed significantly better on higher-order questions (HOQs) than the control, suggesting a greater benefit for tackling complex tasks in some contexts. Confidence was also significantly boosted, especially among low-confidence students, but the impact varied by module. The effects in the respiration and cell division modules were less pronounced. Overall, the study highlights the effectiveness of metacognitive strategies in promoting both content understanding and confidence, especially for students with low initial confidence, but their effectiveness appears to depend on contextual factors. The results underscore the importance of tailoring these strategies to diverse topics or content, and individual learning needs to maximize their effectiveness.

TI Assessing the Evolving the Culture of Biology program through the lens
   of the Teacher-Centered Systemic Reform model
SO JOURNAL OF MICROBIOLOGY & BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE teaching assistant teaching professional development; Teacher-Centered
   Systemic Reform; teaching assistant training; graduate students
ID UNDERGRADUATE SCIENCE; COLLEGE; ASSISTANTS; EDUCATION; STUDENTS;
   BARRIERS; ANATOMY; SUPPORT
AB There are persistent national calls to advance evidence-based instructional practices to increase the number of students graduating with science degrees. Evolving the Culture of Biology is a program designed to improve undergraduate education by prioritizing graduate teaching assistant teaching professional development (TA-TPD). Guided by the Teacher-Centered Systemic Reform (TCSR) model, this study examined how TA TPD practitioners' (participants) attitudes, personal factors, institutional contexts, and instructional practices shape TA-TPD reform outcomes. Using a pre-program survey and end-of-year semi-structured interviews, we gained insight into participants' experiences as they developed and implemented reformed TA-TPD. We investigated how TCSR components differentially influenced participant progress, and whether consistent patterns emerged among reform approaches, barriers, and outcomes. Contextual factors, dissatisfaction with previous programming, and participants' departmental positions in relation to institutional structures emerged as critical influences on implementation and approach. Further analysis led to the development of three institutional team "profiles" to describe TA-TPD reform progress: Long strides, started with minimal to no TA-TPD programming and created substantial growth in TA-TPD infrastructure; Refiners, expanded and updated existing programs, specifically adding lessons on pedagogy; and high-barrier, low buy-in, who faced insurmountable barriers that prevented the ability to reach reform goals.

TI Shifting Incentives and Academic Priorities: The Effects of
   Responsibility Center Management (RCM) on Degree Outcomes
SO RESEARCH IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Higher education; Finance; Budgets; Responsibility center management
   (RCM); Degree production; Market-oriented policy
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; SCHOOL CHOICE
AB A growing number of public universities in the US have adopted a decentralized budget model known as responsibility center management (RCM). Compared with the traditional centralized budget model, RCM gives greater budgetary responsibility and decision-making to individual academic units, meaning that units take on greater roles in generating revenue and managing costs. Leveraging the staggered adoption of RCM across public universities, this study finds that RCM is positively associated with the production of master's degrees, but negatively associated with the production of doctoral degrees. Field-level differences are found, with the positive effect on master's degrees most evident for STEM, a high-demand field. Transition to a decentralized budget model appears to affect how academic units approach degree production, potentially leading to a greater focus on revenue generation, with the possibility of reinforcing resource disparities across academic fields.
