TI Embodied nursery rhyme teaching shows preliminary efficacy for
   preschoolers' language aesthetic ability: a pilot mixed-methods study
   from China
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE aesthetic abiIity; children's language; embodied cognitive theory;
   nursery rhyme teaching; teaching method
AB Introduction Language aesthetic ability is central to early childhood arts education. However, traditional nursery-rhyme instruction in China often emphasizes rote recitation, neglecting the role of embodied experience. Grounded in embodied cognition theory, this study operationalizes embodied-cognition principles into a four-step teaching model and examines its impact on senior-kindergarteners' language aesthetic development. Methods Using a sequential mixed-methods design, we first interviewed an expert teacher to construct a pedagogical model, then conducted a quasi-experiment in a public kindergarten in Kunming. Two intact senior-kindergarten classes (N = 60, M_age = 5.4 years, SD = 0.3) were randomly allocated at the class level to either an experimental condition (n = 30) receiving 12 30-minute embodied nursery-rhyme sessions or a wait-list control (n = 30) engaged in the standard language curriculum. Language aesthetic ability was assessed pre- and post-intervention using a self-developed observation scale (Cronbach's alpha = 0.70). Results Gain-score analysis revealed significantly greater improvement in the experimental group than in the control group (Delta M +/- SD = 5.50 +/- 1.87 vs. 2.00 +/- 1.34), t(58) = 8.332, p < 0.001. The mean gain-score difference between groups was 3.50 points [95% CI (2.66, 4.34)], with a large effect size (Cohen's d = 2.14). Discussion Embodied nursery-rhyme instruction was associated with significant gains in preschoolers' language aesthetic ability and offers a culturally responsive illustrative model warranting replication for kindergarten aesthetic education. Study limitations include the small, culturally homogeneous sample and short intervention period. Future studies should adopt multisite designs and long-term follow-ups to test generalizability and sustainability. These findings should be interpreted as exploratory efficacy evidence from a single-site, researcher-led pilot, pending confirmation in larger, independent trials.

AB Introduction: This study investigated the effectiveness of multimedia resources integrated with local cultural content in teaching English narrative texts to Indonesian EFL students. The study aimed to examine whether multimedia materials based on local folk stories could enhance students' reading comprehension, understanding of narrative elements, and engagement in learning. Methods: The study employed a one-group pre-test-post-test quasi-experimental design supported by a descriptive survey. The participants were 40 ninth-grade students aged 14-15 from a public secondary school in Indonesia. The intervention utilized videos and e-books containing local cultural narratives. Data were collected through a reading comprehension test, a narrative element comprehension test, and a 15-item Likert-scale questionnaire measuring engagement in terms of attitudes, interest, and motivation. The pre-test and post-test scores were analyzed using paired-samples t-tests, while the questionnaire data were analyzed descriptively. Results: The findings revealed significant improvements in students' reading comprehension, which increased from the pre-test (M = 84.03, SD = 2.96) to the posttest (M = 86.83, SD = 3.45), t(39) = 4.914, p < .001, Cohen's dz = 0.78. Students' understanding of narrative elements also improved significantly from the pre-test (M = 82.65, SD = 4.15) to the post-test (M = 84.95, SD = 5.81), t(39) = 3.269, p = .002, Cohen's dz = 0.52. In addition, the questionnaire results demonstrated positive learner engagement, with mean scores of 3.98 for attitudes, 3.89 for interest, and 3.72 for motivation. Discussion: The findings suggest that multimedia resources enriched with local cultural content can effectively support both cognitive and affective dimensions of EFL narrative learning. The integration of multimedia learning and culturally responsive pedagogy contributed to improved comprehension, narrative understanding, and learner engagement. This study provides pedagogical implications for EFL teachers seeking to incorporate culturally meaningful multimedia resources into narrative text instruction.

TI Exploring student engagement with video-based assessments in a large
   software engineering course
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE active learning; computer science education (CSE); large class groups;
   software engineering education (SEE); student engagement;
   student-created artifacts; student-created videos
AB Active learning in large-scale computer science (CS) courses remains challenging, particularly when supporting student engagement and understanding at scale. Courses with hundreds of students often rely on automated activities and summative assessments that prioritize grading efficiency over reflective learning, which can contribute to anxiety, frustration, and misconceptions when students learn complex topics and technologies. To explore alternative assessment practices, this paper reports on a learner-centered strategy grounded in learning by teaching, in which students created instructional videos as part of a course assessment. We examine students' self-reported perceptions of learning, effort, and performance and compare video assessments with traditional test-based formats to inform assessment design in large CS courses.

TI Efficacy of AI virtual tutors in emotional self-regulation for children
   and adolescents (ages 6-18)
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article

   inclusion
AB Background: The current study is concerned with the efficiency of AI virtual tutor 'TEAMIGO' in the development of emotional self-regulation in children and adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). Method: After the single-arm longitudinal design without a control group, we managed to obtain a sample consisting of 110 subjects (including 55 participants with ASD and 55 with ADHD) within the age range of 6-18 years. TI Gender, teaching experience, and ICT integration self-efficacy in
   economics classrooms: evidence from Ghanaian senior high schools
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE economics education; gender differences; ICT integration; self-efficacy;
   teaching experience
ID COMPUTER ANXIETY; TECHNOLOGY; UNIVERSITY; ATTITUDES; STUDENTS; INTERNET
AB Introduction The integration of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) into teaching and learning has become a central strategy for improving instructional effectiveness and student engagement in secondary education. However, the extent to which Economics teachers and students in Ghana possess the confidence to use ICT effectively, and whether such confidence differs by gender and teaching experience, remains underexplored. This study examined the ICT integration self-efficacy of Economics teachers and students in Ghanaian Senior High Schools, with particular attention to gender differences among teachers and students and variations associated with teachers' years of teaching experience.Methods Guided by Self-Efficacy Theory, the study adopted a quantitative approach using a descriptive cross-sectional survey design. The sample comprised 350 Economics students and 40 Economics teachers. Data were collected using an adapted version of the Computer Technology Integration Survey. Descriptive statistics (means and standard deviations) were used to assess levels of ICT integration self-efficacy, while inferential statistics (independent samples t-tests and analysis of variance [ANOVA]) were employed to examine gender and teaching experience differences.Results and Discussion The findings revealed that both teachers and students reported high levels of ICT integration self-efficacy. No statistically significant gender differences were found among teachers and students in their self-efficacy for using ICT in teaching and learning. In addition, teaching experience did not significantly influence teachers' ICT integration self-efficacy. The findings suggest that, although overall confidence in ICT use is high, schools should provide continuous professional development and practical training focused on emerging digital tools and pedagogical ICT integration. These results offer useful insights for policymakers and educational stakeholders seeking to strengthen ICT integration in Ghanaian Senior High Schools.

TI Digital technology integration for developing research competence in
   primary school students
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION

DT Article
DE digital inquiry; digital pedagogical design; digital research products;
   digital technologies; inquiry-based learning; Kazakhstan; primary
   education; quasi-experimental study
ID PEDAGOGICAL CONTENT KNOWLEDGE
AB Introduction This study examines how a structured digital pedagogical design supports the development of research competence among primary school students in Kazakhstan. Research competence is understood as an age-appropriate ability to formulate questions, work with information, organize evidence, use digital tools purposefully, and present simple inquiry-based conclusions.Methods The study used a quasi-experimental non-equivalent control group pretest-post-test design with 118 Grade 3-4 students: 59 in the control group and 59 in the experimental group. Discussion The findings suggest that digital technologies may support research competence when they are embedded in guided inquiry, teacher mediation, formative feedback, and aligned assessment, rather than used as separate technical tools. Urban and rural/small-rural subgroups both improved under the intervention, although contextual differences remained.

TI Co-creating custom GPTs: an autoethnographic study of undergraduate
   students as partners in generative AI innovation
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE co-creation; custom GPTs; generative AI; reflective practice;
   students-as-partners; undergraduate education
AB This study explores how undergraduate students co-created and evaluated custom Generative AI (GenAI) tools within a students-as-partners (SaP) framework. Undergraduate participants, within a Summer Scholarship program and in a placement coursework unit, collaborated with academic staff to design, test, and refine custom Generative Pre-trained Transformer chatbots (cGPTs), aligned with pedagogical goals. By embedding partnership pedagogy into GenAI co-creation, this study offers a model for more inclusive, critical, and transformative engagement with emerging technologies in university settings.

TI Technology acceptance and social justice in rural higher education: a
   qualitative study of learning management systems and curriculum delivery
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE curriculum delivery; learning management systems; qualitative research;
   rural higher education; social justice theory; technology acceptance
   model
ID DISABLED STUDENTS; USER ACCEPTANCE
AB Introduction This qualitative study investigated how undergraduate pre-service teachers at a rural, historically disadvantaged university in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, experience and navigate the use of the institutional Learning Management System (LMS) for curriculum delivery. It specifically examined the extent to which structural and institutional conditions enable or constrain equitable LMS participation.Methods Using purposive sampling, 40 undergraduate students enrolled in a Bachelor of Education programme were selected to represent varying year groups, socio-economic backgrounds, and LMS engagement levels (determined via self-reports and lecturer interaction patterns). Data were collected over six weeks through semi-structured interviews (45-75 minutes) in private or neutral venues. Trustworthiness was ensured via a 14-week data engagement period, member checking with a subsample ($n = 4$), peer debriefing, and reflexive journaling. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, combining inductive coding with a deductive phase drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Social Justice Theory.Results The findings indicate that while pre-service teachers recognize the LMS as an essential tool for accessing learning materials, assessments, and communication, meaningful engagement is severely constrained by structural inequalities. These include limited device access, unreliable internet connectivity, prohibitive data costs, and inadequate institutional support. Viewed through a social justice lens, these challenges reflect systemic failures in redistribution, recognition, and representation.Discussion The study reveals a critical disconnect between technological acceptance and educational equity, demonstrating that positive perceptions of LMS functionality are insufficient without enabling material and institutional conditions. By utilizing an integrated TAM-Social Justice framework, this study advances existing scholarship by demonstrating how individual technology acceptance is deeply mediated by, and cannot be disentangled from, structural inequity.

TI Mathematical literacy: mother-tongue intervention for measurement errors
   and misconceptions
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE errors; mathematical literacy; mother-tongue instruction; mathematical
   misconceptions; multilingual education
ID LANGUAGE
AB Introduction This empirical study explores teachers' perspectives on the pedagogical role of the mother tongue in mitigating errors in Measurement. Although the cognitive benefits of mother-tongue instruction are widely acknowledged, limited research has examined how teachers distinguish between surface-level linguistic decoding and the deeper process of conceptual sense-making. The study argues that learners' heritage languages should be understood not as temporary translation devices, but as continuous cognitive resources that mediate conceptualisation in Mathematical Literacy.Methods A qualitative interpretivist case study was adopted, involving semi-structured interviews and 12 classroom observations with 6 purposively selected teachers across diverse performance contexts, couched in Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory, which conceptualizes the mother tongue as a cultural tool for scaffolding learning within the Zone of Proximal Development. The findings emphasize the need for structured multilingual pedagogies and improved linguistic resources to enhance equitable conceptual access in the unique South African educational landscape.

TI Secondary level students' linguistic competencies for learning English
   in community schools: a narrative case study of Sindhupalchok district
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE linguistic competence; learning english; secondary students; narrative
   study; community school
AB Introduction The present study examines the linguistic competencies of secondary-level students, focusing on their proficiency in English and the reasons for their varying English learning outcomes. The purpose of this study is to gain a deeper understanding of how the linguistic backgrounds of secondary students have shaped their English learning.Methods This paper employs a qualitative narrative case study method and an interpretative research paradigm to explore the linguistic competencies of secondary students learning English at three community schools in the Sindhupalchok district of Bagmati Province, Nepal. The study selects three participants, two male and one female student, using a purposive sampling procedure for data collection. This paper uses open-ended questionnaires to conduct narrative interviews, analyzes reviewed documents, and develops meanings based on the most frequent themes synthesized from participants' transcribed narratives.Results The findings show that the secondary students of community schools in Sindhupalchok, Nepal, have been challenged with different aspects: socio- economic factors, teachers' command of English, and the learning atmosphere of English in any informal setting, like home, neighborhood, and the entire place of residence. Similarly, those students' intrinsic motivation and management of supportive, resourceful, and motivating environments both at school and home directly influence their development of linguistic competencies in English. The study also talks about the relationship between Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory and Communicative Language Teaching in shaping students' learning routes. Participants' stories focus on the importance of digital platforms like YouTube and social media as informal learning tools, yet uneven access to technology causes participants' inequalities in English learning. Peer interactions and teacher-student collaborations are highlighted as important but underused options for practicing English, along with Krashen's emphasis on comprehensible input.Discussion The study highlights the relationship between Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory and Communicative Language Teaching in shaping students' learning routes. Therefore, the present study suggests addressing these challenges and differences to improve English linguistic competencies and provide equitable educational opportunities for all students.

TI Transitioning to active learning in veterinary medical education:
   post-pandemic reflections from veterinary students and faculty
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE accreditation; andragogy; epidemiology; flipped; online learning; public
   health; veterinary medicine
ID COVID-19; TECHNOLOGY
AB Introduction: The COVID-19 pandemic promulgated a palette of digital practices that subsequently transformed global higher education. In this study, we explored the experiences of veterinary students and faculty on the abrupt shift to online learning during the COVID-19 pandemic, which initially posed unprecedented challenges to the institution. This disruption not only highlighted gaps in digital readiness but also forced an exploration of new teaching strategies. The study's findings informed the adjustment of teaching approaches, away from a purely didactic model to the use of digital tools within the Sakai Learning Management System (LMS) to support active learning and student engagement. Methods: The study drew on three main sources of data to explore students' learning activity and experiences in online courses during the pandemic. The usage patterns of the Sakai (LMS) among 112 students were evaluated across the twelve courses taught from 2020 to 2021. Secondly, qualitative data were collected from student focus groups and faculty focus groups. Formal end of term course evaluations for courses in veterinary epidemiology and veterinary public health were also collected from students. Results: Transitioning to virtual learning during the pandemic prompted revisions to pedagogy and training to use digital technologies in the online classroom. The training in the use of digital tools for education increased faculty confidence in embedding technology in their courses upon their return to the island following the pandemic. Subsequently, the knowledge gained about the engagement capabilities of the various aspects of the LMS led to a critical assessment of teaching methods, away from purely didactic approaches towards digital tools that could promote active learning and student engagement. Conclusion: The study offers actionable insights and digital practices implemented within the Doctor of Veterinary Medicine (DVM) program, shaped by exposure to online learning during the COVID-19 pandemic. These practices include the use of flipped classroom approaches, an instructional model that consists of pre-class preparation for in-class applications aligned with learning outcome-based assessments. The lessons learned during the pandemic led to more extensive use of various features within the Sakai LMS. The latter, coupled with case-based and peer learning sessions, led to the redesign of two courses led by the primary investigator, veterinary epidemiology and public health, underscored by theoretical frameworks such as motivational theory and andragogy.

TI A commognitive perspective on the use of mathematical vocabulary in a
   discursive mathematics classroom
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE commognition theory; discourse; discourse analysis; mathematics
   vocabulary; mathematical discourse
ID KNOWLEDGE; LANGUAGE; CHILDREN; ENGLISH; 3RD
AB Introduction Mathematics vocabulary is an essential aspect of mathematical language that enables learners to participate effectively in classroom discourse; however, few studies have examined its development within classroom discourse from a commognitive perspective. This study addresses this gap by offering a commognitive account of the mathematical vocabulary used in a discursive mathematics classroom.Methods Using a qualitative ethnographic research design, data were generated through classroom observations and document analysis and examined using commognition theory as both a theoretical framework and a methodological lens for discourse analysis. The participants comprised 25 learners and their mathematics teacher, selected through purposive sampling.Findings The findings indicate that the mathematical vocabulary in use encompassed both colloquial and technical registers and evolved from routine, phrase-driven usage towards increasingly objectified forms, signalling a more formalized understanding of mathematical objects.Discussion The study contributes to the literature by illuminating how discourse mediates learners' transition from process-oriented to product-oriented participation in mathematical discourse, a shift that supports the development of mathematical proficiency. The results underscore the importance of teachers' deliberate scaffolding of mathematical vocabulary and their use of precise, consistent terms that promote equitable access to the understanding of mathematical concepts. Furthermore, the study highlights discourse-based mathematics learning as a critical pathway for deepening conceptual understanding through language.

TI Reconceptualizing teacher preparation for gifted learners in inclusive
   education: differentiation as a structuring principle of professional
   readiness
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE differentiated instruction; future teacher preparation; gifted learners;
   inclusive education; professional readiness; teacher education
ID EFFICACY; PEDAGOGY
AB The article examines teacher preparation for working with gifted learners in inclusive education by positioning differentiated instruction as a structuring principle of professional readiness. The study aimed to develop and pilot a theoretically grounded preparation model that connects inclusive pedagogy, gifted education, and differentiated instructional design within a unified framework of teacher education. The empirical part of the study used a one-group pretest-posttest pilot design with future teachers from two universities in Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. The final matched sample included 79 participants who completed a semester-based module focused on differentiated support for gifted learners in heterogeneous classrooms. The module addressed giftedness as a dynamic and context-sensitive developmental phenomenon and included work with learner profiles, cognitively complex tasks, flexible pacing, enrichment, formative assessment, and socio-emotional responsiveness. The results showed statistically significant within-group increases in self-reported professional readiness across the measured domains. The most pronounced gains were observed in gifted-specific readiness, particularly in identifying and developing gifted potential, designing cognitively complex tasks, and managing differentiated instruction and assessment. Regression analysis indicated that gains in gifted-specific readiness were most strongly associated with improvement in differentiated instructional readiness. Within the limits of a one-group self-report pilot design, the findings suggest that preparation for inclusive gifted education may need to move beyond general inclusive attitudes toward a more differentiated pedagogical repertoire. Such preparation may support future teachers in connecting participation, challenge, support, and socio-emotional responsiveness in mixed-ability classrooms. The study contributes to teacher education research by offering preliminary evidence on differentiation as an operational link between inclusive education and gifted education. Its conclusions remain cautious, as the study relied on self-report measures and did not include a control group, random assignment, observed teaching practice, or direct learner-level outcomes.

TI Sex differences in emotional exhaustion among higher-education students
   during the pre-vaccination COVID-19 period: evidence from Chile and the
   ECE interpretive framework (ECE-Int)
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE burnout; COVID-19; ECE-Int; emotional exhaustion; emotional exhaustion
   scale (ECE); sex differences; university students
ID SOCIAL STRESS TEST; GENDER-DIFFERENCES; BURNOUT; PERFORMANCE; MEN;
   WOMEN; LABOR; REACTIVITY; EMPLOYEES; RESPONSES
AB Emotional exhaustion (EE), the core dimension of burnout, has emerged as a particularly detrimental outcome, yet limited research has examined its incidence and severity by sex or provided tools to interpret its symptomatological manifestations. This study pursued two objectives: (1) to determine the incidence and severity of emotional exhaustion in Chilean higher-education students during the pandemic, disaggregated by sex; and (2) to develop and apply an interpretive framework for the Emotional Exhaustion Scale (ECE), organizing scores into cognitive, affective, and social-interactional domains. A quantitative, cross-sectional, correlational design was employed, using a non-probabilistic snowball sample of 1,301 students who completed a digital questionnaire that included sociodemographic items, contextual information, and the ECE. Data collection was conducted between August and November 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, prior to the availability of vaccines. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, independent-samples t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and exploratory stepwise multiple linear regression analyses. Results showed that 87.4% of students presented high or very high emotional exhaustion. Females reported significantly higher exhaustion than males (40.7 +/- 7.69 vs. 36.7 +/- 9.36; t(1,299) = 4.00, p < 0.001), with 90.5% of females vs. 77.4% of males in the high/very high categories. Regression analyses identified sex, GPA, age, and study schedule as significant predictors, though the explained variance was modest (R-2 = .076). The ECE-Int framework contextualized total scores, showing that high EE was associated with clusters of cognitive (e.g., concentration and memory problems), affective (e.g., anxiety, irritability, depressive symptoms), and social-interactional (e.g., withdrawal, interpersonal conflict) indicators, particularly among females. By combining sex-disaggregated analyses with a complementary interpretive framework, this study extends prior research in Chilean higher education contexts and offers an interpretive approach to understanding emotional exhaustion in this context.

TI Pedagogical opportunities, school manager literacy, and managerial
   potential among pre-service teachers in Kazakhstan: a latent class
   analysis
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE latent class analysis; managerial potential; pedagogical opportunities;
   school manager literacy; teacher education; teacher leadership
ID LEADERSHIP
AB Cultivating leadership capabilities and managerial competencies among pre-service teachers has become an important objective of contemporary teacher education programs. This study examines pedagogical opportunities for the development of leadership-related competencies and managerial readiness among pre-service teachers. Data were collected from 220 pre-service teachers, enrolled in two universities in Kazakhstan, through a structured survey consisting of three scales measuring pedagogical opportunities, school manager literacy, and managerial potential. Latent class analysis was conducted separately for each scale to identify distinct response profiles among participants. The results revealed three latent profiles of pedagogical opportunities (strong, moderate, and limited), two profiles of school manager literacy (high and relatively lower), and three profiles of managerial potential (very high, high, and moderate). Most respondents belonged to profiles reflecting strong pedagogical opportunities and high managerial competence, indicating generally positive perceptions of leadership readiness among pre-service teachers. The findings suggest that most pre-service teachers perceive themselves as possessing relatively strong managerial competencies and leadership potential, although variations exist in the availability and perception of pedagogical opportunities during teacher education. The findings suggest that teacher education programs can better prepare pre-service teachers for leadership roles by more systematically integrating leadership training and school-based experiences.

TI Asynchronous-first as an ethical imperative: rethinking time, presence,
   and equity in teacher professional development
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE asynchronous learning; bichronous design; equity; in-service teachers;
   interrupted trajectories; online learning; teacher professional
   development; temporal justice
AB Professional development for in-service teachers has long assumed synchronous participation as the pedagogical norm, positioning asynchronous formats as pragmatic concessions to logistical constraint. This Perspective Paper develops the notion that asynchronous-first design is not a compromise but an ethical imperative, grounded in recognition of the structural realities of teachers' professional and personal lives. Drawing on scholarship on interrupted academic trajectories, time poverty, equity in online learning, and the political economy of professional learning, the article advances three interrelated claims: that synchronous participation carries hidden costs disproportionately borne by practitioners navigating care responsibilities and precarious employment; that asynchronous formats enable forms of cognitive engagement that synchronous delivery constrains; and that access to professional learning should not be conditional on temporal availability. Implications for accreditation policy, micro-credential design, and the selective use of optional synchronous moments are discussed. The article repositions asynchronous-first design as evidence of institutional commitment to equity rather than accommodation of constraint.

TI Validating a four-factor model of teachers' online assessment practices
   in the UAE tertiary education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE assessment design; assessment improvement; assessment literacy;
   assessment practice; CFA; digital assessment literacy; EFA; TOAP
ID ASSESSMENT LITERACY; FIT INDEXES
AB Online assessment has largely become a structural component of tertiary education in different contexts, yet limited empirical evidence exists on how university teachers design, implement, interpret, and use online assessment as a coherent multidimensional construct. This study examined teachers' online assessment practices (TOAP) in Emirati tertiary education context and evaluated the factorial structure, reliability, and model fit of a 31-item TOAP inventory. Using a cross-sectional survey, we collected data from 314 faculty members across multiple academic departments. Our findings showed that the full TOAP inventory demonstrated strong internal consistency, alpha = .931, and the revised factors also showed strong reliability and adequate convergent validity. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) suggested a more complex empirical structure than the original four-domain framework, with evidence of overlap among some indicators. Based on the inconsistent results we obtained from EFA, we decided to use confirmatory factor analysis to test a revised four-factor model comprising Assessment Improvement, Assessment Design, Assessment Practice, and Assessment Literacy. The revised model retained all 31 indicators and demonstrated strong model fit: chi 2 (428) = 420.092, p = .598; chi 2/df = .982; RMR = .041; GFI = .921; AGFI = .909; CFI = 1.000; TLI = 1.002; RMSEA = .000; and PCLOSE = 1.000. The findings supported TOAP as a coherent multidimensional framework in which teachers' use of assessment evidence, online assessment design, enacted assessment practices, and assessment literacy are related but distinguishable domains. The study siuggested a validated diagnostic framework for strengthening professional development in online assessment, particularly in validity-oriented design, feedback quality, rubric use, moderation, fairness, and AI-resilient assessment practices.

TI The contested landscape of foundational learning data in Cameroon
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Cameroon; data; education policy; foundational learning; political
   economy
AB Background Access to reliable foundational learning data is crucial for enhancing educational outcomes, especially in light of the global learning crisis, where, despite a substantial increase in school enrolment, many children are not acquiring basic skills such as literacy and numeracy. In Cameroon, access to foundational learning data is deeply contested, with stakeholders facing significant barriers that limit data access, sharing, and use.Methods This study employed a mixed-methods design, integrating a structured survey of 287 respondents, complemented by 87 key informant interviews and a focus group discussion with 26 participants. The participants included educators, ministry officials, researchers, local administrators, community leaders, and civil society organizations. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative data were coded thematically in MaxQDA. The analysis was structured around barriers and facilitators to accessing foundational learning data.Results The results reveal a landscape characterized by parallel systems of data collection, profound mistrust among stakeholders, and systematic barriers to accessing data that are driven by competing political and institutional interests. While formal hierarchical structures and digital platforms facilitate data access, they are undermined by resource scarcity, political interference, armed conflict, and a culture of data hoarding.Conclusion Improving foundational learning outcomes requires not just better data systems, but a reconfiguration of the political and institutional arrangements that govern how educational data is produced, shared, and used. This study contributes to understanding education data ecosystems in contexts of fragility and offers insights for policymakers, donors, and practitioners working to strengthen evidence-based education planning.

TI From performance to shared responsibility? School self-evaluation and
   accountability in a territorial education policy
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational inequality; school self-evaluation; shared accountability;
   TEIP programme; territorial disparities
ID IMPROVEMENT; JUSTICE
AB School self-evaluation has become a central instrument for school accountability and improvement in contemporary education systems and plays a key role within Portugal's Educational Territories of Priority Intervention programme (TEIP), which supports schools in socially and territorially vulnerable communities. This study examines how school self-evaluation (SSE) has been embedded within this programme, as well as how it relates to persistent territorial inequalities in educational outcomes. This study combines document analysis of official TEIP monitoring and evaluation reports with secondary analysis of retention and dropout rates from the Directorate-General for Education and Science Statistics. The findings indicate that SSE has evolved from an initially implicit reflective practice into an institutionalized reporting mechanism closely aligned with indicator-based internal evaluation and centralized monitoring cycles. Evidence also shows that TEIP schools consistently present higher retention and dropout rates than national averages, together with considerable variation across border municipalities, pointing to the continuing influence of territorial conditions in educational outcomes. The study concludes that governance structures prioritize redistributive monitoring of measurable outcomes while providing more limited institutional space for contextual recognition and participatory representation, suggesting the need for more context-sensitive and collaborative accountability approaches to strengthen SSE's potential to support equitable educational improvement.

TI Lexical precision in police blotters: an adjective-based forensic
   linguistic analysis and its implications for English for specific
   purposes
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE appraisal theory; attributive adjective; criminology education; English
   for specific purposes; forensic linguistics; institutional collocation;
   police blotter
ID LANGUAGE
AB Police blotters are primary legal documents that initiate documentary chains extending through criminal investigations, prosecutions, and judicial proceedings. Research on police incident reports has demonstrated that officer word choices, whether intentional or not, can signal attitudinal stances that influence investigative and prosecutorial outcomes. Despite their evidentiary significance, the linguistic choices embedded in blotter narratives, particularly adjectival usage, have received limited systematic attention. This study examines how adjectives function in English-written police blotters from Tacloban City, Philippines, and derives pedagogical implications for the design of the English for Specific Purposes (ESP) curriculum in criminology education. Using a qualitative descriptive design with textual evaluation analysis, ten purposively sampled police blotters from two police stations (2019-2022) were coded for syntactic position, semantic category, and collocational patterning. Adjectives occurred overwhelmingly in attributive position within dense noun phrases, forming institutionalized collocations such as initial investigation, physical injury, and lawful arrest that function as genre-specific phraseological units. Several adjectives also carried evaluative loading, notably intoxicating liquor and unidentified cohort, with the potential to frame suspects and events in legally consequential ways. These findings support the integration of corpus-informed ESP modules in criminology programs that address attributive adjectival usage, institutional collocation, and the ethical distinction between precision-serving and bias-introducing adjective choices. The study contributes to forensic linguistics, ESP pedagogy, and criminology education by providing an empirically grounded analysis of the lexical register of local police documentation.

TI Measuring engagement in technology-supported collaborative argumentative
   writing: Development and validation of the T-CLEA scale
SO ASSESSING WRITING
LA English
DT Article
DE Writing assessment; Engagement; Technology-supported collaborative
   writing; EFL argumentative writing; Scale development; Higher education
ID MEASURING STUDENT ENGAGEMENT; WRITTEN CORRECTIVE FEEDBACK; ENGLISH;
   LANGUAGE; SCHOOL; STATE
AB Current moves toward AI-supported and collaborative writing environments highlight the need for validated instruments that assess learners' engagement in technology-mediated argumentative writing. This study developed and validated the Technology-supported Collaborative Learning Engagement Assessment (T-CLEA) scale, a bilingual English-Mandarin self-report instrument for university EFL courses involving digitally supported collaborative argumentative tasks on Sustainable Development Goal topics. T-CLEA comprises three task-specific dimensions: English Writing Challenges (EWC), Student Issues on Global Topics (SIG), and Perceptions of Collaborative Argumentation (PCA). Items were generated from relevant theories and empirical studies, refined through expert review, translated and back-translated, and pilot tested. Internal consistency was good across dimensions (Cronbach's alpha =.87-.89; CR =.87-.89), and convergent and discriminant validity evidence supported the construct structure. T-CLEA offers a contextsensitive diagnostic tool for examining engagement, writing quality, and process-based indicators in technology-supported EAP/EFL writing contexts.

TI Comparison of learning gain across face-to-face, mixed, and live online
   participation in a HyFlex National Pharmacist Examination Preparation
   Course: A controlled four-month comparative study
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE HyFlex course; Face-to-face instruction; Live online instruction;
   Pharmacy education; National Pharmacist Examination
ID STUDENTS; QUESTIONNAIRE; EDUCATION
AB Introduction: In Japanese pharmacy education, success on the National Pharmacist Examination is a key objective. This study evaluated learning gain across face-to-face, mixed-attendance, and live online participation patterns in a four-month HyFlex National Pharmacist Examination preparation course under controlled conditions. Methods: Sixth-year pharmacy students at Musashino University, Tokyo, Japan, participated in a four-month HyFlex course and chose their attendance mode for each session. Students with >= 90% attendance who completed the pre- and post-course examinations were classified as face-to-face (>= 75% in-person attendance), live online (>= 75% online attendance), or mixed-attendance (<75% in either modality). Learning gain was defined as the post-course examination correct-answer rate (%) minus the pre-course examination correct-answer rate (%). Results: The overall cohort (n = 208) showed a learning gain of 16.9 +/- 0.5%. Learning gain was 20.2 +/- 1.2% in the face-to-face group (n = 23), 16.4 +/- 0.8% in the mixed-attendance group (n = 41), and 16.5 +/- 0.6% in the live online group (n = 144). Learning gain tended to be higher in the face-to-face group than in the mixed-attendance group (p = 0.061; d = 0.736) and was higher than in the live online group (p = 0.028; d = 0.546), whereas the mixed-attendance and live online groups showed nearly identical learning gain (p = 0.998; d = 0.010). Conclusions: These findings support the educational value of HyFlex as a flexible learning environment. Face-to-face participation was associated with greater learning gain than live online participation, whereas mixed-attendance and live online participation showed similar learning gain.

AB This study uses mixed methods to examine how participation in a Quality Rating and Improvement System (QRIS) may support site leaders' confidence, well-being, and quality improvement efforts. To address an important gap in the existing literature, the study includes the experiences of ECE leaders across settings, including home-based family child care (FCC) and family, friend, and neighbor (FFN) providers who are often overlooked in research and policy. Data include site leader survey data (n = 367), coach survey data (n = 26), and interview data from 10 case study sites. Findings suggest improvements in site leaders' confidence, perceptions of stress, and site-level classroom quality in the context of QRIS participation, with qualitative themes illuminating the role of workplace relationships in supporting leaders' well-being. Together, these findings suggest that QRIS may serve as a promising mechanism for supporting program quality and the well-being of the diverse leaders who drive it.

TI Facilitating adaptive learning: A QCA study on conditions for learning
   in simulation games
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Learning conditions; Effect study; Simulation games; Interventions;
   Facilitation; Facilitation design; Qualitative comparative analysis
   (QCA); Adaptive learning
ID QUALITATIVE COMPARATIVE-ANALYSIS; TECHNOLOGY; MODEL
AB Background Research on how facilitation design and facilitator interventions influence adaptive learning outcomes in simulation games remains limited. While previous studies have examined individual learning conditions in simulation games, less is known about how these conditions operate in combination to support adaptive learning. Aims This study investigates which combinations of facilitation design conditions and facilitator interventions enhance adaptive learning outcomes in simulation games. Samples The study analyses 31 simulation game cases from educational and organizational contexts. Methods A Qualitative Comparative Analysis (QCA) was conducted to examine configurations of five learning conditions: buy-in (buyin), expectancy guidance (expect), intervention approach (interv), learning loops (loops), and debriefing setup (debrf). Data were retrieved from multiple sources, including session transcripts, interviews with facilitators and participants, session reports, questionnaires, in-game assessments, and reflection materials. Results Two intermediate configurations leading to adaptive learning outcomes were identified. Configuration 1 consisted of buyin(& lowast;)expect(& lowast;)loops similar to debrf, while Configuration 2 consisted of buyin(& lowast;)interv(& lowast;)loops(& lowast;)debrf. The parsimonious solution (buyin(& lowast;)loops) indicates that buy-in and learning loops constitute core conditions across configurations linked to the outcome. Necessity analysis further shows that expect and interv also function as necessary conditions, although they appear in different configurations. Debriefing does not emerge as a necessary condition and contributes to the outcome only within specific configurations. Conclusions These findings provide insight into how facilitation design conditions interact in simulation games and offer guidance for preparing facilitation strategies that support adaptive learning.

TI The clinical communication competence and influencing factors among
   undergraduate nursing interns: A latent profile analysis
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Undergraduate nursing students; Interns; Clinical communication
   competence; Latent profile analysis; Influencing factors
ID STUDENTS; MANAGEMENT; FRAMEWORK; EDUCATION; ABILITY; STRESS; SKILLS;
   MODEL
AB Background: Clinical communication competence is fundamental to patient-centered care and underpins nursing interns' ability to build trust and navigate complex clinical interactions. Exploring the heterogeneity of communication competence among undergraduate nursing interns and its associated factors may inform the development of personalized training strategies to enhance their clinical preparedness. Aim: To identify the potential subgroups and influencing factors of clinical communication competence among undergraduate nursing interns. Design: A cross-sectional study. Methods: A total of 312 undergraduate nursing interns were selected and surveyed using a demographic questionnaire, the Clinical Communication Competence Scale, and the Chinese version of the Ten-item Big Five Personality Inventory. The clinical communication competence of these undergraduates was classified using latent profile analysis, and the predictors of profiles were explored using multivariate logistic regression analysis. Results: The average score for clinical communication competence among nursing interns was 80.21 +/- 15.16 (range: 30-112), indicating a moderate-to-high level of competence overall. The participants were divided into three latent profiles: the low communication competence group (7.4%), the medium communication competence group (78.5%), and the high communication competence group (14.1%). The personality traits of conscientiousness and extraversion, proactively choosing the nursing major, and previous experience in interpersonal communication training were positively associated with higher clinical communication competence among nursing interns, with statistical significance (P < 0.05). Conclusions: Undergraduate nursing interns' clinical communication competence is heterogeneous and mostly at a medium level. To enhance this, nursing educators and clinical nursing managers should strengthen students' professional identity, boost interpersonal communication learning, and design communication training approaches tailored to students' distinct dispositional profiles.

TI Unpacking the heterogeneity of AI literacy among nursing undergraduates:
   A latent profile analysis
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing students; Latent profile analysis; AI literacy; Critical
   thinking; Professional identity
ID SELF-DETERMINATION
AB Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming healthcare, making AI literacy an essential competency for future nurses. However, variable-centered studies may overlook heterogeneity in nursing students' AI literacy. Objectives: To identify latent profiles of AI literacy among nursing undergraduates and examine demographic and psychological factors associated with profile membership. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 342 nursing undergraduates recruited by convenience sampling. AI literacy was measured using the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale. Latent Profile Analysis was performed based on 12 scale items, and multinomial logistic regression was used to examine associated factors. Results: Three AI literacy profiles were identified: Moderate AI Literacy Profile (48.0%), Passive Adopters with Low Ethical Vigilance Profile (36.8%), and High AI Literacy Profile (15.2%). Critical thinking positively predicted membership in the High AI Literacy Profile (OR = 5.196, p < 0.001), whereas lower family income (<2000 CNY) reduced the likelihood of belonging to this profile (OR = 0.073, p = 0.018). Higher learning motivation decreased the likelihood of membership in the Passive Adopters with Low Ethical Vigilance Profile (OR = 0.484, p < 0.001), while higher professional identity increased the likelihood of belonging to this profile (OR = 1.484, p = 0.017). Conclusions: Nursing undergraduates showed heterogeneous AI literacy profiles rather than a simple low-to-high pattern. Critical thinking and socioeconomic resources were associated with higher AI literacy, while professional identity alone may not ensure balanced AI literacy development. Tailored educational strategies are needed to strengthen AI knowledge, critical thinking, autonomous learning motivation, ethical awareness, and equitable access to AI-related learning resources.

TI Students' eye-movement behaviors in solving physics problems with
   different information structures
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID ARITHMETIC WORD-PROBLEMS; IRRELEVANT INFORMATION; STRATEGIES; TRACKING;
   COMPREHENSION; MATHEMATICS; ATTENTION; KNOWLEDGE; CHILDREN
AB Students' problem-solving processes have attracted a wide range of attention. From an information processing perspective, we distinguish three types of physics problems: information-explicit, information-redundant, and information-implicit. This study explores students' visual behaviors when they were doing problem solving with these three types of problems. The participant sample included 90 high school students. Eye-tracking technology was used to record their eye movements while they solved each type of problem. The results showed that although students' accuracy did not differ significantly across the three problem types, their eye-movement behaviors exhibited differences. Students displayed longer total fixation times on information-redundant problems, particularly in the text and option areas, suggesting increased cognitive effort caused by extraneous information. In contrast, information-implicit problems elicited the highest number of revisits to the text area, indicating students' repeated attempts to extract obscured information. Moreover, students devoted more fixation time and more revisits to the correct option in information-explicit problems, whereas information-redundant and information-implicit problems resulted in longer fixation and more revisits to incorrect options. These findings indicated that students' visual attention patterns were influenced by the information structures of the physics problems, even though their performance outcomes did not significantly differ. The study highlights the importance of problem design in supporting students' effective reasoning and information integration.

TI Assessment fairness in higher education: Examining achievement,
   differential item functioning, and perceptions of exam fairness
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Assessment fairness; Differential item functioning; Perceptions of exam
   fairness; Test anxiety; Higher education
ID CLASSROOM ASSESSMENT; VALIDITY; BIAS
AB This study examined assessment fairness in higher education by integrating psychometric and perceptual evidence. Data were obtained from 177 preservice teachers enrolled in the Faculty of Education at a state university during the 2025-2026 academic year. The dataset included an achievement test, an exploratory exam fairness perception form, and a test anxiety measure. Item and test statistics, 2 & times; 3 factorial ANOVA, logistic regression-based differential item functioning (DIF) analyses, and factorial MANCOVA controlling for anxiety were conducted. Results showed that the achievement test had generally acceptable psychometric properties. Achievement scores differed significantly across department groups, but not by gender or the gender & times; department interaction. No significant DIF was detected by gender, whereas only one item showed significant DIF across departments. Anxiety was significantly associated with procedural and structural fairness perceptions. Overall, the findings indicate that assessment fairness should be evaluated through both psychometric quality and students' perceived fairness.

TI Longitudinal associations between generative AI feedback perception and
   academic achievement: A comparative analysis of evaluative and
   instructional feedback
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI feedback; Evaluative feedback; Instructional feedback;
   Academic achievement; Emotional intelligence; Longitudinal study
ID MULTIDIMENSIONAL SCALE; PERFORMANCE; VALIDATION; POWER
AB Generative AI feedback (evaluative and instructional information produced by large language models in response to student submissions) has become increasingly common in higher education, yet longitudinal evidence on how students' perceptions of such feedback are associated with academic outcomes remains limited. This three-wave study examined the differential and interactive associations of evaluative and instructional generative AI feedback perception with academic achievement among 6030 Chinese first-year undergraduates, assessed at three time points across consecutive semesters. Cross-lagged panel models showed that evaluative feedback perception was positively associated with subsequent achievement (beta =.31 and beta =.28, p < .001), whereas instructional feedback perception showed non-significant direct associations. Random intercept cross-lagged panel models confirmed these within-person patterns. The evaluative feedback-achievement association was partially statistically mediated by perceived social support (39.4% of total association), while instructional feedback was fully mediated through this pathway (68.3%). Emotional intelligence moderated these associations in a compensatory pattern, with stronger associations among students with lower emotional intelligence. The evaluative & times; instructional feedback interaction was positively associated with achievement at the second time point (beta =.150, p = .018), with instructional feedback showing significant associations only under high evaluative feedback conditions. This interaction varied across disciplines. These findings extend feedback theory to generative AI contexts and offer preliminary recommendations for integrated AI feedback design.

TI ASTRA: A synthetic benchmark for trace-based evaluation of socially
   intelligent multi-agent tutoring and participation-balanced
   collaboration in introductory programming
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI; Introductory programming; Multi-agent tutoring;
   Collaborative learning; Pair programming; Learning analytics; Trace
   data; Synthetic benchmark dataset
AB Generative AI is rapidly entering introductory programming, yet evidence about how learners coordinate with AI, especially in dyads, remains limited, and open datasets that support reproducible, trace-based evaluation are scarce. I present ASTRA (Adaptive Socially-intelligent Team Reasoning Agents), a multi-agent tutoring pro totype and benchmark framework for studying collaborative programming with socially differentiated agents. ASTRA supports three configurations: alone_tutor (one learner with a Tutor agent), pair_tutor (two learners with a Tutor agent), and pair_multiagent (two learners with Tutor and Facilitator agents, where the Facilitator prompts coordination and balanced participation). As access to research participants is not yet available, I release an open synthetic benchmark dataset that mirrors ASTRA's logging schema and a prespecified between-subjects design (N = 540 participants; 360 sessions; 1440 task episodes) across a bank of 20 short Python programming tasks. The dataset includes turn-level dialogue traces and task-level artefacts designed to support log-operational research questions about interaction dynamics, participation balance and reciprocal engagement in dyads, and performance and verification behaviours. Descriptive summaries and illustrative models indicate that the bench mark yields measurable condition-differentiated patterns consistent with the simulation assumptions. I emphasise that these findings are simulated evidence intended for benchmarking, measurement feasibility, and reproducible pipeline development, not causal estimates of learning effects, while providing a transparent analysis blueprint for future ethics-approved validation studies.

TI More often or longer? The effects of the academic schedule on
   postsecondary academic outcomes
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic schedule; Postsecondary schedule; Biweekly classes;
   Postsecondary outcomes
ID SCHOOL START TIME; STUDENT PERFORMANCE; ACHIEVEMENT; IMPACT
AB One of the most common scheduling decisions in higher education is the determination of biweekly or triweekly classes. On the surface, these two formats are equivalent in terms of the number of minutes in a course (75 min twice a week or 50 min three times a week). However, the two structures may have different pros and cons for both students and faculty, and it is ambiguous which course format should yield better student outcomes. We leverage more than a decade's worth of administrative transcript data from a large public university in the Midwest to examine the effects of the academic schedule on postsecondary student outcomes. Across a range of model specifications employing department, faculty, course, and student fixed effects, we find that when a student enrolls in a triweekly class, they earn lower grades and are less likely to take a subsequent course in that same field. These effects are especially pronounced in the STEM fields, where we also find negative effects of the triweekly schedule on students' eventual choice of major.

TI Content validation of a psychosocial self-management intervention to
   reduce depressive symptoms in older adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus
SO EDUCACION MEDICA
LA English
DT Article
DE Type 2 diabetes mellitus; Depressive symptoms; Self-management;
   Psychosocial intervention; Content validity; Older adults
ID RISK-FACTORS
AB Introduction: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) in older adults is frequently associated with depressive symptoms that hinder effective self-management and worsen health outcomes. Psychosocial interventions integrating emotional and educational components are needed, and their content validity must be established to ensure relevance, clarity, and theoretical coherence. Materials and methods: A mixed-methods approach was used, incorporating expert judgment from nine healthcare professionals with expertise in diabetes education and intervention. The content validity was assessed using a Likert-type rubric and the Program Fit Assessment Tool, focusing on clarity, relevance, pertinence, coherence, alignment with community context, and theoretical framework. Results: The intervention demonstrated overall adequate content validity, although specific areas for improvement were identified, particularly regarding certain session topics and time management. Experts recommended strengthening the emotional components of the intervention and improving clarity in communication. Conclusion: The intervention was deemed appropriate for older adults with T2DM, aligning with their needs. This validation process contributes to the development of more effective and culturally sensitive psychosocial strategies, potentially improving self-care and mental health outcomes in this population. TI Assessing ICT integration in civic education: Barriers, enablers and
   practitioner perspectives in Ghana
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Ghana; Assessing; Barriers; Technology; ICT policy; Integration; Civic
   education
AB This study explored the enabling and hindering factors of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) in civic education delivery, while addressing an empirical gap in the literature. Adopting a pragmatic philosophical approach, we conducted one-on-one interviews with 22 civic education practitioners across six geographical districts in Ghana. The data collected were analysed using thematic analysis guided by the People-ProcessTechnology Model. The study revealed three key barriers: insufficient technical infrastructure, inadequate pedagogical training, and organisational policy constraints. The average self-rating of ICT integration in civic education was five out of ten (5/10). Participants recommended increased investment in ICT infrastructure, targeted professional development, and policy reforms to address the barriers identified by the practitioners. Based on these findings, we conclude that providing technological support and training to civic educators is essential to ensure both immediate and long-term improvements in civic education delivery in the studied districts in Ghana.

TI Exploring differences between the work of degree qualified early
   childhood teachers and non-degree qualified educators in Australian
   exemplary early childhood education and care settings
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Early childhood teachers; Early childhood education and care; Time use;
   The theory of practice architectures; Work
ID DISPOSITIONS
AB This mixed-methods study examines differences in the work of degree-qualified early childhood teachers (ECTs) and other qualified educators in exemplary Australian early childhood education and care (ECEC) settings. Amid workforce shortages and mixed evidence about ECT impact, international policy continues to position ECTs as central to quality, yet research rarely distinguishes educators by qualification. Using the theory of practice architectures, the study investigates how ECTs' work differs, and what organisational conditions enable practice. Data were generated through time-use diaries (n = 321; 3610 hours), focus groups and interviews (111 participants), ten case studies, and a survey (n = 82). Findings show clear distinctions in ECTs' practices, dispositions (knowledge, skills and values) and emotional experiences. ECTs spend more time on planning, assessment, and pedagogical leadership, supported by cultural-discursive, material-economic and socio-political arrangements. By differentiating ECT contributions and enabling conditions, the study fills a critical research gap and informs workforce and quality policy within Australia and beyond to the international sphere.

DE Generative artificial intelligence; Interdisciplinary thinking;
   Epistemic network analysis; Management education; Socio-constructivism;
   Human-machine collaboration
AB Management education increasingly asks students to work across disciplinary boundaries when addressing complex business problems. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may support this work by scaffolding information search, problem framing, and cross-functional reasoning, but it also raises concerns about uncritical reliance and reduced independent evaluation. This study examines a pedagogically tuned GenAI intervention as a cognitive mediator in team-based management learning. In a mixed-methods randomized controlled trial, 84 MBA students assigned to 28 teams solved an ill-structured strategic case with either a customized GenAI partner or traditional search resources. The analysis combined rubric-based evaluation of final team reports, team-level epistemic network analysis (ENA) of collaborative discourse, and post-task interviews. AI-supported teams produced higher-quality strategic reports, with higher scores especially for interdisciplinary integration and innovation. ENA showed that these teams also displayed more densely connected discourse patterns linking information retrieval, cross-disciplinary reasoning, integrative synthesis, and critical evaluation. Interview data suggest that the AI partner helped teams move some low-level information-foraging work into a more evaluative and synthetic discussion mode. Rather than supporting generic GenAI use, the results highlight the value of human-in-the-loop tasks that combine scaffolded inquiry, peer discussion, and assessment of reasoning processes alongside AI-assisted products.

ID ACADEMIC LANGUAGE; KNOWLEDGE
AB Understanding and expressing attitudinal meanings in English with precision and sophistication in everyday and academic contexts is an important aspect of highly proficient English language competence necessary for teaching in English as the Medium of Instruction (EMI). It has been a great challenge for learners of English as an additional language including those enrolled in tertiary TEFL (Teaching English as a Foreign Language) programs. After the interventions, the study found a significant improvement in the students' evaluative language expressions, including those whose original assessment result was classified as low achieving. Not only the students' evaluative language expressions were improved, their metalanguage of APPRAISAL was also developed. They were able to use the metalanguage to justify and evaluate their own deployment of ATTITUDE and GRADUATION in different writing tasks. The outcomes of this study have implications for TEFL and EAP teaching of aspects of advanced English proficiency required of English Medium Instruction teachers as well as for, English textbook design and the assessment of English language competencies in EFL.

TI Exploring staff perceptions of gender attainment gaps: A case study
   within a Post-92 United Kingdom university sports department
SO JOURNAL OF HOSPITALITY LEISURE SPORT & TOURISM EDUCATION

DT Article
DE Attainment gap; Gender; Higher education; Sport students; Staff
   perceptions; Undergraduate
ID ACHIEVEMENT
AB Research shows that globally, women/girls academically outperform men/boys across educational levels. Yet despite high enrolments onto UK sports degree programmes, limited research has investigated staff views on this matter. This study explored academics' perceptions of gender-related attainment gaps within undergraduate sport programmes at a post-92 university. TI Development of working memory through childhood: The interplay of family
   socioeconomic status and parenting behaviors
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Socioeconomic status; Working memory; Parenting behaviors; Family
   process
ID EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS; ADOLESCENT RESILIENCE; MATURATION; CHILDREN;
   SCHOOLS; POVERTY; STRESS
AB This study examined the interplay between family socioeconomic status (SES) and parenting behaviors on the developmental trajectory of working memory (WM) from kindergarten to the fifth grade. Using latent growth modeling with data on 15,437 children from the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study, Kindergarten Class of 2010-11(ECLS-K:2011), we revealed that higher SES was associated with better initial WM, slower WM growth rate, and hysteretic deceleration in WM development. Cognitive stimulation moderated the association between SES and WM development. Parental warmth and spanking did not moderate the association between SES and WM development. These findings highlight the importance of cognitive stimulation in buffering the adverse impacts of low SES on WM development. The findings have implications for the design of interventions to foster cognitive competence in children from disadvantaged backgrounds.

TI Digital competence and functional requirements for a digital learning
   and knowledge platform for evidence-based nursing: A mixed-methods study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital competence; Evidence-based practice; Nursing; Digital health;
   Mixed-methods; Knowledge platforms; DCQ; Self-report questionnaire;
   Austria
AB Background: Digital technologies are central to healthcare quality and safety, requiring nurses to develop digital competence to access and apply evolving evidence in practice and education. Digital learning and knowledge platforms play a key role in nursing education and continuing professional development, yet little is known about prioritized functions and differences across qualification and educational pathways. Objectives: To identify and prioritize functional features of a digital learning and knowledge platform for evidence-based nursing and to assess the digital competence of Austrian nurses and nursing students across sociodemographic and professional groups. Methods: An explanatory mixed-methods study was conducted. First, an online survey (n = 238) assessed functional requirements, knowledge sources, and digital competence using the Digital Competence Questionnaire for Nurses (DCQ). Group comparisons and multiple regression models were performed. Second, semistructured interviews (n = 7) explored contextual factors shaping platform use and evidence access. Results: Nurses prioritized fast retrieval functions - search (87.4%), filters (78.2%) - and visibility of new or updated content. Texts (90.8%) and short videos (86.1%) were preferred formats, with younger participants showing greater interest in interactive elements. Registered nurses and those outside direct care more frequently used formal evidence sources, while assistants and direct-care staff relied more on training and peer exchange. Digital competence was high overall (M = 4.31 on a 5-point scale, higher values indicating greater competence), with assistants scoring lower than registered nurses. Interview participants emphasized the importance of transparent source referencing, visible update cycles, efficient navigation, just-in-time support, device accessibility, and learning-oriented design features for platform usability and trustworthiness. Conclusions: Across roles and settings, nurses emphasize rapid, trustworthy, and concise access to evidence. Platform design should prioritize transparent provenance, visible recency, and role-relevant filtering while offering diverse content formats. Qualification-related differences may point to varying support needs and tailored entry routes, particularly for assistant roles.

TI Dynamic changes and relationships among AI Literacy, job crafting, and
   career growth in new nurses in the AI era: A multicenter three-wave
   longitudinal study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE AI literacy; Job crafting; Career growth; New nurse
ID OF-FIT INDEXES; MODEL
AB Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are being rapidly integrated into the nursing field. As a new and emerging force within the nursing workforce, new nurses face both opportunities and challenges in their career growth in the AI era. AI literacy has become increasingly important and may play a critical role in shaping the career growth of new nurses. However, research examining the dynamic changes, influencing factors, and underlying mechanisms of career growth among new nurses in the context of AI remains limited. Objective: To explore the dynamic trajectories of AI literacy, job crafting, and career growth among new nurses, and to examine the longitudinal mediating role of job crafting in the relationship between AI literacy and career growth. Design: A multicenter, three-wave longitudinal study. Methods: The AI Literacy Scale, Job Crafting Scale, and Career Growth Scale were administered in April 2025 (T1), July 2025 (T2), and October 2025 (T3) to 339 new nurses from five tertiary general hospitals across different regions of China. SPSS 26.0 and AMOS 26.0 were used to construct longitudinal mediation models and conduct data analyses. Results: Across T1, T2, and T3, the mean scores of AI literacy and career growth showed a pattern of initial decline followed by an increase over time, whereas the mean score of job crafting demonstrated a continuous upward trend. At all time points, AI literacy, job crafting, and career growth were significantly and positively correlated. AI literacy positively predicted career growth in new nurses, and job crafting played a significant longitudinal mediating role in this relationship. Conclusions: AI literacy among new nurses can predict their future career growth through the mediating role of job crafting. Hospitals and nursing educators should attach importance to AI-related training and guidance for new nurses and strive to create organizational environments characterized by appropriate autonomy and support. Encouraging reasonable job crafting is crucial for fostering career growth among new nurses in the AI era and for promoting the sustainable development of the nursing profession.

TI The role of liberal and conservative thinking in innovation: a SEM
   analysis of physical education teachers
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Liberal thinking; Conservative thinking; Innovation; Physical education
   teacher
ID MENTAL SELF-GOVERNMENT; STYLES; BEHAVIOR; CREATIVITY; MODEL
AB Physical education is an additional field of education that promotes the physical, social and emotional development of students and academic education. In this field, physical education has introduced innovative knowledge and practices and innovative ways of working have been made possible. On the other hand, thinking leaning plays an important role in shaping teachers' understanding of innovation and practices. This study explored the relationship between thinking leaning and innovative workplace behavior. This study selected a descriptive and cross-sectional design, in which 849 Turkish physical education teachers participated, and examined the relationship between variables using structural equation modeling. Data were collected using a liberal and conservative thinking style scale and an innovative work behavior scale. Structural models showed that the liberal thinking style positively and strongly predicted the innovative working practices of physical education teachers, while the conservative style negatively predicted and weakly. Therefore, there is a structurally strong relationship between thought styles and innovative work behavior. In this structure, it has been observed that, in particular, the liberal thinking style plays an important role in the innovative work behavior of physical education teachers. This study highlights the role and importance of liberal and conservative thinking styles in education, even in different cultural contexts, and shows that these types of thinking remain effective in the development of innovation strategies. In this sense, the value of liberal thinking should be highlighted in the development of innovative educational environments.

   competencies; Large-scale assessments in education
ID COLLABORATION; TEACHERS; SYSTEMS
AB Teaching competencies are a fundamental element in promoting quality, equitable education. This paper aims to analyse how teaching competencies relate to academic achievement and educational equity. Using the PISA 2018 database, comprising a representative sample of 35,943 students and 21,621 teachers in Spain, the study proposes a multilevel predictive model of academic performance (at the student and school levels) based on teaching-related factors. TI Zoo visits as catalysts for science identity: informal learning and
   career aspirations among grade 3-7 students in South Africa
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Informal learning; Science-related aspiration; Zoo education; Social
   cognitive career theory; Possible selves theory; Primary education
ID FIELD TRIPS
AB Informal learning experiences can spark dreams that classroom lessons alone may not ignite. This qualitative study investigated how a zoo visit influenced the science-related career aspirations of Grade 3-7 students in South Africa. Guided by social cognitive career theory and possible selves theory, the study explored students' experiences of engagement, meaning-making, and emerging aspirations through interviews, drawings, and classroom observations with 25 students and five teachers from five schools. Findings revealed that the zoo visit stimulated high levels of enthusiasm, enriched scientific understanding, and inspired students to imagine futures as scientists, veterinarians, and conservationists. The study emphasises the potential of informal learning environments to shape early science identities and aspirations, suggesting that stronger connections between informal experiences and classroom learning could help nurture a more diverse and motivated future science-related workforce.
