TI Parental responsiveness and punishment in preschoolers' cooperation and
   aggression through emotional competencies: A four-wave multilevel study
   in Taiwan
SO EARLY CHILDHOOD RESEARCH QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE Aggression; Cooperation; Emotional competencies; Multilevel modeling;
   Parental responsiveness; Parental punishment
ID SOCIAL COMPETENCE; HARSH DISCIPLINE; MODERATING ROLE; WARMTH;
   ADJUSTMENT; CHILDHOOD; CHILDREN; BEHAVIORS; KNOWLEDGE; CONTEXT
AB Parenting is a dynamic process that shapes preschoolers' socio-emotional adjustment, yet few longitudinal studies distinguish within-person changes from stable between-person differences when examining cooperation and aggression. Guided by emotion socialization theory, this study tested whether parental responsiveness and punishment were associated with Taiwanese preschoolers' cooperation and aggression and whether these associations were mediated by emotional competencies. Using four annual waves of national cohort data from 2,103 Taiwanese children (1,025 girls, 1,078 boys) aged 3-6 years, multilevel models separated within- from between-person variation. At the between-person level, higher parental responsiveness was associated with greater cooperation and lower aggression, whereas parental punishment was associated only with higher aggression. At the within-person level, increases in parental responsiveness predicted later increases in cooperation and decreases in aggression, whereas increases in parental punishment predicted the opposite pattern. Mediation analyses showed differentiated emotional pathways. For parental responsiveness, between-person mediation emerged through emotional expression and regulation for greater cooperation and through emotional awareness and regulation for lower aggression, whereas within-person mediation emerged only for increased cooperation through emotional expression, understanding, and regulation. For parental punishment, between-person mediation was limited and mixed, operating through emotional regulation for both lower cooperation and greater aggression and unexpectedly through emotional expression for greater cooperation, whereas no within-person mediation was supported. These findings extend emotion socialization theory by showing that parenting relates to preschoolers' social adjustment through distinct between- and within-person pathways and by clarifying the selective mediating role of emotional competencies in contemporary Taiwan.

TI The effect on crime of extending the school day in secondary education:
   Evidence from the Dominican Republic
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE School-day extension; crime; risk behavior; Dominican Republic
ID ADVERSE CHILDHOOD EXPERIENCES; JUVENILE CRIME; INCAPACITATION; ADULTS
AB This paper studies the impact of a school-day extension on crime. Specifically, we analyze the Jornada Escolar Extendida (JEE) program in secondary education in the Dominican Republic, which doubled the length of the school day in public schools, and exploit its staggered rollout across municipalities over time. TI Technology-enhanced learning environments in Central Asian higher
   education: A four-study, multi-institutional quasi-experimental research
   program (N=945)
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Technology-enhanced learning; Learning management systems; Artificial
   intelligence in education; Competency-based education; Medical
   education; Quasi-experimental study; Central Asia
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; MEDICAL-EDUCATION; ENGAGEMENT; MODEL
AB The rapid digital transformation of higher education in Central Asia proceeds despite a scarcity of large-scale, multi-site empirical evidence comparing technology-enhanced learning (TEL) environments with traditional instruction. To address this gap, this study evaluated whether TEL environments improve learning outcomes and student engagement across diverse populations, institutions, and technology layers, and assessed whether these effects scale with the depth of technological integration. Conducted between 2023 and 2026 across five higher education institutions in Uzbekistan (N = 945), the methodology employed four quasi-experimental parallel-group sub-studies. Sub-study 1 (n = 503) compared a Moodle-based methodology against traditional instruction across three pedagogical institutes. Sub-studies 2 (n = 120), 3 (n = 124), and 4 (n = 198) examined progressively integrated TEL approaches at a medical institute, ranging from content-competency blended learning to AI-driven adaptive learning with virtual laboratories, and AI-enhanced analytics with intelligent assessment. Outcomes were measured using expert-validated 100-point standardized scales. Findings indicated that the experimental groups significantly outperformed control groups across all four sub-studies (p < 0.001). Effect sizes increased with depth of TEL integration: from a moderate efficiency gain in Sub-study 1 (eta approximate to 1.11) to very large effects in Sub-studies 2-4 (Cohen's d = 1.93-3.29; Hedges' g = 1.88-3.20), with the most pronounced improvements observed in digital literacy and clinical decision-making. Student engagement indicators were also consistently higher in the TEL cohorts. Ultimately, these results demonstrate that TEL environments significantly enhance learning outcomes, with gains scaling alongside technological complexity. The findings support a contextually conditional framework for TEL adoption within credit-modular systems, contingent upon robust infrastructure, faculty readiness, data-governance capacity, and established ethical safeguards.

   Dynamic mathematics software; Lower secondary education
ID SELF-EFFICACY; MATH ANXIETY; ACHIEVEMENT; TECHNOLOGY; ATTITUDES;
   SOFTWARE; IMPACT; SLOPE
AB This study investigated the effects of GeoGebra-supported instruction on eighth-grade students' cognitive, affective, and social engagement, as well as their mathematics anxiety. A quasiexperimental pretest-posttest control group design was employed with 62 eighth-grade students (experimental group, n = 32; control group, n = 30) from a public middle school in northwestern T & uuml;rkiye. The control group received traditional textbook-based instruction on linear equations and slope, whereas the experimental group engaged with the dynamic mathematics software, GeoGebra. Data were collected using the Student Engagement in Mathematics Scale (SEMS), Mathematics Anxiety Scale (MAS), and a student opinion questionnaire form. Quantitative data were analyzed using SPSS, whereas qualitative data were analyzed using content analysis techniques. Quantitative analyses revealed that GeoGebra-supported instruction significantly increased cognitive, affective, and social engagement and concurrently reduced math anxiety. Qualitative findings indicated that dynamic visualizations, interactive manipulation of variables, immediate feedback, and collaborative activities enhanced conceptual understanding, supported exploratory learning, and alleviated students' mathematics anxiety. These results highlight GeoGebra as an epistemic learning environment in which engagement and affective regulation mutually reinforce each other. Overall, this study demonstrates that dynamic mathematics software-supported instruction can simultaneously enhance cognitive, affective, and social engagement while reducing mathematics anxiety among middle-grade students.

AB The rising enrolment of international students in higher education worldwide brings both opportunities and challenges, particularly for those in teacher education programs, who face professional experiences where cultural, linguistic, and pedagogical differences intersect. TI Accounting graduates' work readiness in the digital era: A
   dual-perspective analysis of technical, information technology, and soft
   skill competencies
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Accounting education; Graduate employability; Soft skills; Technical
   competency; IT competency
ID PERCEPTIONS; EMPLOYERS; TRENDS
AB This study examines the roles of technical accounting, information technology (IT) and soft skill competencies in shaping accounting graduates' work readiness from the perspectives of final-year students and prospective employers. Using a dual-survey design, data were collected from 208 graduating accounting students and 113 employers in Beijing and Shanghai through the Sojump platform. The data were analysed using SPSS and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (SmartPLS). The findings suggest that students who report higher levels of technical accounting competency, IT competency, and soft skills also perceive themselves as more workready. From the employers' perspective, technical accounting competency and soft skills are positively associated with the importance placed on work readiness, whereas IT competency does not significantly influence employers' evaluations. The findings reveal a divergence between students' self-perceived competencies and employers' evaluative priorities regarding work readiness. This study contributes to employability research by offering a complementary understanding of how work readiness is formed and interpreted across stakeholder groups. Overall, our findings suggest that accounting education should move beyond generic IT instruction, instead prioritizing applied digital competencies alongside technical and interpersonal rigor to better align graduates with labour market expectations.

TI Beyond tools to teammates: A multilevel study of explainable ChatGPT in
   virtual team learning
SO INTERNET AND HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Explainable AI; Social presence; Human-AI teams; Virtual team learning;
   Self-regulated learning
ID TECHNOLOGY; COHESION; TRUST
AB Conversational agents are shifting from solo tutors to teammates in online project-based learning, yet little is known about how design features shape dynamics. Drawing on self-regulated learning and volitional control theory, we examine how ChatGPT affects team learning. A survey of 356 students nested in 48 teams tests a model linking AI explainability to intention to continue learning via perceived social presence, with team perceived virtuality and cohesion as moderators. Explainability heightens the agent's social presence, and this copresence boosts intention to continue learning. High virtuality and cohesion strengthen this pathway. Social presence is pivotal, and we offer design recommendations for embedding explainable AI in teamwork.

TI Exploring EFL undergraduate students' critical AI literacy in academic
   writing
SO JOURNAL OF ENGLISH FOR ACADEMIC PURPOSES
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI; Critical AI literacy; English for academic purposes;
   Academic writing; Second language writing
AB The rapid development and deployment of generative artificial intelligence (AI) have significantly impacted the field of English for Academic Purposes, offering valuable opportunities for enhancing L2 academic writing while also raising notable challenges. To harness the benefits of AI, the concept of critical AI literacy has emerged as a vital construct for understanding students' abilities to critically evaluate AI tools, effectively use them for specific tasks, and engage with them ethically. To illuminate this emerging concept and inform pedagogical practices, the present study investigates the enactment of critical AI literacy among Chinese EFL undergraduates in an academic writing context. Data were collected from 16 undergraduate students enrolled in an English academic writing course, using multiple sources such as students' drafts, AI interaction logs, guided reflective journals, and semi-structured interviews. The findings illustrate a nuanced enactment of students' critical AI literacy, characterized by their heightened critical awareness of AI's affordances and limitations, critical strategies in orchestrating the AI-mediated writing process, critical evaluation of AI outputs against academic writing standards, and critical negotiation of ethical boundaries to safeguard authorial integrity. The study underscores the pedagogical imperative to foster students' critical AI literacy in academic writing by integrating interdependent skill dimensions, tailoring instruction to learners' developmental stages, and pairing explicit AI-use guidelines with process-focused activities in L2 writing classrooms.

TI Relationships between psychosocial aspects of stuttering and
   self-disclosure of stuttering in a Japanese sample
SO JOURNAL OF FLUENCY DISORDERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Developmental stuttering; Self-disclosure; Self-stigma; Assessment;
   Psychosocial issues; Japanese
ID SPEAKERS EXPERIENCE; ADULTS; ADOLESCENTS; PERCEPTIONS; SPEECH; ESTEEM;
   IMPACT; STIGMA; THERAPY; SCALE
AB Purpose: We aimed to psychometrically evaluate a Japanese version of the Disclosure of Stuttering Scale, from Boyle et al. (2018), and identify the psychosocial factors associated with level of stuttering self-disclosure among adults who stutter. Methods: Adults who stutter were recruited via stuttering self-help groups in Japan and the authors' contacts. Participants completed their demographics, the Disclosure of Stuttering Scale and other psychological scales assessing affective, cognitive, and social aspects of stuttering via an online survey. We analyzed 180 participants after those with unreliable or duplicate responses were excluded. The scale's reliability and validity were confirmed, and multiple linear regression analysis was conducted to predict the score of the Disclosure of Stuttering Scale using demographic variables and psychological measures. Results: The Japanese Disclosure of Stuttering Scale had good internal consistency (omega =.832) and test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient =.808), with no obvious ceiling or floor effects. Level of self-disclosure of stuttering was lower in the Japanese sample than in the United States sample (Cohen's d = 0.55) reported by Boyle et al. (2018). The regression model revealed that self-reported male gender, self-help group experience, higher self-acceptance, and lower selfstigma were associated with a higher self-disclosure level (adjusted R2 =.347). Conclusion: Our study indicated that self-reported gender and psychological and social (self-help experience) components were associated with the level of self-disclosure of stuttering. Furthermore, Japanese adults who stutter tended to report lower levels of self-disclosure compared to previous samples, which may reflect sociocultural differences.

TI Efficiently building the essential skill of letter sound fluency: A
   randomized controlled trial of a technology-based activity
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Letter sound fluency; Incremental rehearsal; Personalized instruction;
   Instructional technology; Early reading intervention
ID INCREMENTAL REHEARSAL; READING-COMPREHENSION; KINDERGARTEN; WORDS;
   METAANALYSIS; INSTRUCTION; MNEMONICS; KNOWLEDGE; CHILDREN; PROGRAM
AB This study was a randomized controlled trial conducted with 82 kindergarten students who were at or below the 50th percentile in letter sound fluency. Students were randomly assigned to a control group (business as usual) or an intervention group where students engaged in letter sound fluency practice using a cloud-based personalized system of instruction for letter sounds (PSI-LS) in which letter sounds were presented via a modified incremental rehearsal (IR) practice schedule. Students participated in a total of 12 sessions across 3 to 4 weeks. Students in the PSI-LS condition did significantly better on measures of letter sound knowledge (d = 1.06), letter sound fluency (d = 1.25), and nonsense word fluency (d = 1.06) than peers in the control condition at posttest. The potential for technology to make instruction activities such as IR more efficient, effective, and individualized is discussed.

TI Effects of Force Feedback on Trainee Performance: A Pilot Study of the
   dV5 Surgical Robot
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE force feedback; robotic-assisted surgery; da Vinci; training
ID INVASIVE SURGERY; VIRTUAL-REALITY; SKILLS
AB INTRODUCTION: Lack of tactile sensation remains a limitation of robotic operations. The da Vinci 5 (dV5) surgical system uses force feedback (FFB) technology, allowing surgeons to sense forces exerted at the instrument tips. Limited studies report that FFB reduces excessive instrument force and enhances tissue manipulation. However, its role in trainee technical performance remains poorly characterized. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of FFB on trainee performance using validated technical rating scales. METHODS: Participants in this pilot study included 4 trainees with varying levels of robotic experience (medical student, intern, clinical fourth year resident, advanced minimally invasive fellow). Each participant performed a simulated robotic lymphadenectomy on the dV5 console, twice with the aid of FFB and twice without. Performances were recorded and subsequently blinded for analysis by 6 faculty reviewers across 6 surgical specialties. Modified Robotic Objective Structured Assessment of Technical Skills (r-OSATS) and Global Evaluative Assessment of Robotic Skills (GEARS) were used to measure respect for tissue, instrument handling, and force sensitivity. Scores were compared across trainees with and without FFB using t-tests and ANOVA. Interobserver agreement among surgeon evaluators was assessed. RESULTS: Across all participants, there were no significant differences in mean GEARS (14.81 vs 12.75, p = 0.4) and r-OSATS (14.25 vs 12.50, p = 0.5) scores between tasks performed with and without FFB. However, in the FFB group, median GEARS (14.8, interquartile range [IQR] 5.5) and r-OSATS (14.5, IQR 3.1) scores were higher compared to the non-FFB group for GEARS (12, IQR 7.5) and r-OSATS (10.8, IQR 7.5). Overall performance scores differed significantly for both GEARS (p = 0.02) and r-OSATS (p = 0.003) when stratified by training level, with more experienced trainees scoring higher. Out of all trainees, only the medical student experienced a wide difference in performance, with higher average GEARS (15.50 vs 8.50) and r-OSATS (14.75 vs 8.50) scoring with FFB, though only r-OSATS was statistically significant (p = 0.172 and p = 0.026). Interobserver agreement among evaluators was fair at r = 0.5. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that novice trainees may experience benefit with FFB in the early learning curve of robotic skill acquisition. Future large-scale studies are warranted to understand the impact of FFB on trainee skill acquisition in robotic surgery.

TI Resident Involvement in Hand Surgery Does Not Impact Operative
   Efficiency or Short-Term Postoperative Complications: A
   Propensity-Matched Study
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE complications; education; hand surgery; orthopedics; outcomes; resident
ID PARTICIPATION; ARTHROPLASTY; FRACTURES; FIXATION; FUSION; LEVEL; TIME
AB OBJECTIVE: In the academic training environment, hand surgeons are tasked with the challenge of teaching operative skills to trainees and balancing efficiency with more complex surgical procedures. In light of a lack of evaluation regarding resident involvement during common hand surgical procedures, we sought to evaluate whether resident involvement in hand surgery cases affects postoperative complication rates and efficiency. DESIGN: Retrospective, matched case-control study evaluating patient demographics, comorbidities, operative times, lengths of stay (LOS), and short term (30-day) postoperative complications for hand surgery cases involving a resident assistant versus surgeon only. SETTING: Nationwide evaluation of surgeons and residents who assisted during carpometacarpal (CMC) arthroplasty for basal joint arthritis and distal radius fracture open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF). PARTICIPANTS: In total, 1752 cases (50% with resident involvement) were included. RESULTS: Overall, 602 patients underwent CMC arthroplasty and 1150 underwent distal radius fracture ORIF, with no difference in demographic or health characteristics between resident only cases versus surgeon only cases. The overall rate of adverse events after hand surgery was 3.25% (57/1752). There were no significant differences in the short-term complication rates in resident-involved (2.5%) versus attending only group (4.0%) (p = 0.105). Total operative times were similar between cohorts (75.8 min versus 74.2 min) (p = 0.563). Lengths of stay were similar between attending only cases and resident involved cases (0.2 vs 0.3 days (p = 0.743). After controlling for patient comorbidities and surgery, resident involvement was not associated with increased odds of postoperative complications. DISCUSSION: Resident involvement in hand surgery is not associated with increased risk for short term (30 day) medical or surgical postoperative complications. Operative efficiency was not impacted by resident involvement during common hand surgery procedures. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III ( J Surg Ed 83:104040. TI A flipped classroom approach compared with low-interactive online
   learning for pediatric pain management knowledge and instructional
   motivation in nursing students: A randomized controlled study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Pediatric pain management; Flipped classroom; Nursing students;
   Instructional motivation; Randomized controlled trial
ID PERCEPTIONS; EDUCATION
AB Aim: This study aimed to compare a flipped classroom approach with low-interactive online learning in terms of nursing students' questionnaire-assessed pediatric pain management knowledge and instructional motivation. Background: Pain management in children is a critical and multidimensional nursing responsibility. However, limited curricular time and opportunities for applied learning may restrict nursing students' preparedness in this area. Structured and interactive instructional formats, such as the flipped classroom, may support knowledge acquisition and motivation in pediatric nursing education. Methods: This study employed a parallel-group randomized controlled trial design with a 1:1 allocation ratio. Eighty-eight third-year prelicensure nursing students were randomized to either the flipped classroom group (n = 44) or the low-interactive online learning group (n = 44). Due to attrition (2 intervention, 2 control), analyses included 42 participants per group (n = 84 in total). Data were collected between February and July 2022 using the Pediatric Pain Management Knowledge Scale for Nursing Students and the Instructional Materials Motivation Survey. This study was prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT07129044). Results: At baseline, the groups were comparable in terms of knowledge and learning motivation. Following the intervention, the flipped classroom group demonstrated greater improvements in questionnaire-assessed pediatric pain management knowledge and instructional motivation than the low-interactive online learning group. Although scores declined from post-test to the three-month follow-up, they remained above baseline in the flipped classroom group. Conclusions: Within the context of this course, the flipped classroom approach was associated with greater improvement in questionnaire-assessed pediatric pain management knowledge and instructional motivation than low-interactive online learning. The findings should be interpreted as proximal educational outcomes rather than evidence of improved clinical competence or durable long-term effectiveness. Further studies using objective performance-based outcomes and longer follow-up periods are needed.

TI Teaching quality: Its influence on student achievement and equity in
   mathematics. Evidence from TIMSS longitudinal
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teaching quality; Mathematics achievement; TIMSS Longitudinal;
   Educational equity; Multilevel modeling; Comparative education
ID CLASSROOM MANAGEMENT; METAANALYSIS; PERCEPTIONS
AB The relationship between teaching quality (TQ) and student achievement remains an ongoing issue in educational research. However, longitudinal evidence is available only for a limited number of countries, whereas international comparative research typically relies on cross-sectional data. Utilizing TIMSS Longitudinal data from 2023 to 2024, this study examines how three TQ dimensions, classroom management, cognitive activation, and supportive climate, predict 2024 mathematics achievement, controlling for 2023 achievement. It further investigates whether class-level socio-economic status (SES) relates to TQ. Multilevel models analyzing primary cohorts (Grade 4/5) in nine countries and lower secondary (Grade 8/9) in three of these countries reveal that supportive climate consistently predicts achievement across both grades, while the impact of cognitive activation is more pronounced in Grade 8/9. At the class level, there were few significant findings for classroom management. Furthermore, descriptive findings show little evidence of systematic SES-related differences in TQ in most participating countries.

TI Do teachers' inclusion-related attitudes and self-efficacy promote
   academic achievement? Results of a longitudinal study
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID PEDAGOGICAL CONTENT BELIEFS; EXPECTANCY-VALUE THEORY; CLASSROOM;
   EDUCATION; STUDENTS; BEHAVIOR; PRESERVICE; PACKAGE; MODELS; SCORES
AB This study aims to examine whether teachers' attitudes toward inclusion and their inclusion-related self-efficacy affect students' academic achievement in reading, spelling, and mathematics in inclusive schools in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. Teachers (N = 217) and students (N = 2079) from 26 schools filled out online and paper-and-pencil questionnaires, respectively, at the beginning and at the end of the fifth grade, just after the transition from primary to secondary school. Results from multi-level regression analyses revealed positive effects of teachers' self-efficacy on students' academic achievement in cross-sectional analyses. Analyses of longitudinal data revealed significant effects of teachers' self-efficacy and attitudes on students' academic achievement in spelling, as well as a significant interaction effect between attitudes and self-efficacy. Against expectations, however, some effects were negative. The results are discussed in the light of the challenges and benefits of promoting inclusive education.

TI Navigating the transnational identity paradox: Attrition and career
   trajectories of Chinese returnee teachers in internationalized schools
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher attrition; Chinese returnee teachers; Internationalized schools;
   Transnational identity paradox; Cognitive dissonance; Career
   trajectories
ID NEGOTIATION; CONFLICT; TURNOVER; NUMBERS
AB Teacher attrition remains a persistent challenge in China's internationalized school sector. This qualitative study examines why Chinese returnee teachers (RTs) leave non-International Baccalaureate (IB) Type C Chinese internationalized schools (CIS) and how they reorganize their careers afterward. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 18 former RTs, the study conceptualizes a Transnational Identity Paradox in which returnees' transnationally shaped professional ideals, pragmatic aspirations for status and mobility, and family-relational obligations become difficult to sustain simultaneously within exam-oriented, commercialized, and stratified school contexts. Using Cognitive Dissonance Theory (CDT) and Identity Negotiation Theory (INT) as analytic lenses, the study identifies four recurring forms of dissonance: pedagogical, professional integrity, status recognition, and family-relational dissonance, which contributed to RTs' attrition decisions. After leaving, participants pursued four post-turnover pathways, including Identity Fortification, Identity Realignment, Identity Retreat, and Identity Reinvention, which functioned as context-bound efforts to reorder competing identities. The findings extend research on teacher attrition, Chinese internationalized schools, and returnee identity by showing how exit can operate as a negotiated response to cumulative and cross-domain identity tension.

TI Global migration model: Applied group project with guided Python code
SO INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF ECONOMICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Python; Programming; Immigration; Inclusive undergraduate teaching;
   Collaborative Online International Learning; (COIL); Active learning;
   Economics
AB Students learn better when they apply their newly acquired knowledge. This paper describes a group project that engages students with a macro-level gravity model of global migration, which incorporates standard push and pull determinants. It includes several proxies for migration costs and accounts for immigration policy. The model is set up and calibrated using publicly available statistics and generates baseline predictions of migration flows for all countries with available data. This project exposes students to basic programming, as more employers seek coding experience among job applicants. No coding experience is necessary and the project is suitable for any class studying international migration. Students can edit the parameters of the model to generate new migration predictions using an interactive, user-friendly experience within Google Colab. The Python code is fully annotated, and students can use an online stepby-step set of guidelines, which is also available in Spanish. Following the completion of the project, students report higher confidence in interpreting migration models (more pronounced among male students) and in working with code (female students in particular).

TI "Everything That Can Be Imagined Is Real": Imagination and Reality in
   Vygotsky
SO CULTURE AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Vygotsky; imagination; thinking; reality; Lenin's Philosophical
   Notebooks
AB An essential dimension of Vygotsky's work on imagination is summed up in the title "everything that can be imagined is real." 1 In the three parts of this paper, it will be shown how this idea is increasingly deepened in Vygotsky's texts. In his earliest writings, he demonstrates that imagination is made up of elements of the real and creates the real. Later on, he adds a new dimension: "crystallized imagination," which enables one to grasp imagination as a cycle. To deepen the relationship between imagination and reality, it is necessary to articulate it with thought. As is shown in part two, a philosophical detour through Lenin reading Hegel in the Philosophical Notebooks enables Vygotsky to design a concept of concept based on imagination. Thought and imagination can thus be conceived as a contradictory unit-as shown in part three-reflecting reality in a zigzag relationship with the real, allowing the construction of the "mentally concrete" [geistig Konkretes].

TI Perfectionistic profiles, achievement goal orientations, and academic
   performance among first-year university students in New Zealand
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Perfectionism; Achievement goal orientations; Academic achievement;
   Latent profile analysis; Person-centred approach; Higher education
ID 2 X-2 MODEL; SCALE FMPS; CONSTRUCT; SELF; ANTECEDENTS; VALIDATION;
   DIMENSIONS; PERFECT
AB This study examined the associations between perfectionism, achievement goal orientations, and academic performance among 1,028 first-year university students in New Zealand. Using latent profile analysis, four distinct perfectionistic profiles were identified: (1) High-Range Mixed Perfectionists with High Family Pressure (high Personal Standards Perfectionism [PSP], high Evaluative Concerns Perfectionism [ECP]), (2) Mid-Range Mixed Perfectionists with Moderate Family Pressure (moderate PSP, moderate ECP), (3) High-Range Mixed Perfectionists with Low Family Pressure (high PSP, high ECP), and (4) Non-Perfectionists (low PSP, low ECP). Profiles characterised by moderate-to-high PSP and ECP with elevated family pressure were more likely to endorse performance-avoidance and work-avoidance goals, whereas High-Range Mixed Perfectionists with Low Family Pressure were more likely to endorse mastery-approach goals and achieved the highest academic performance. Overall, these findings extend person-centred perfectionism research by demonstrating that not only the level, but also the source of evaluative concerns is critical. Specifically, distinguishing between internally regulated and family-driven evaluative pressures provides a more nuanced understanding of how perfectionism relates to students' motivation and academic adjustment in underrepresented educational contexts, such as New Zealand.

AB This study evaluated the impact of a school-based pilot program designed to reduce gender stereotypes and biases in fourth-grade school children. The program used multiple strategies to reduce gender stereotypes and biases relating to social roles and to the agency-communion paradigm. It also aimed to improve egalitarian attitudes. TI Interdependence of context, child- and word-related predictors of
   single-word reading strategies in German-speaking second graders
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Reading strategies; Context; Child-level prerequisites; Word-level
   characteristics
ID LEXICAL QUALITY; INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES; SENTENCE CONTEXT; NAMING SPEED;
   VOCABULARY; COMPREHENSION; RECOGNITION; FREQUENCY; LITERACY; DYSLEXIA
AB This study examined how child- and word-level characteristics as well as contextual information influence reading strategy use and whether there are interdependencies between the levels. German-speaking second graders (N = 124) were assessed on rapid automatized naming and vocabulary. To assess reading strategies, students read individual words aloud, with half of the words being presented with auditory context sentences. Word-level characteristics included frequency and familiarity. A linear mixed-effects model was used to analyze the relationships between context, child-level and word-level characteristics and reading strategies simultaneously. Context, child-level (vocabulary and naming) and word-level (frequency and familiarity) characteristics significantly influenced reading strategy use. Furthermore, interaction effects showed that both naming and vocabulary moderated the influence of context. Multiple factors influence the word reading process. However, these factors are not independent of one another, suggesting that different factors should be considered in reading lessons and reading support to adapt learning units to the specific needs of individual children.

TI A Comparison of Gifted and Typically Developing Children's Friendship
   Relationships, Psychological Well-Being, and Social Problem-Solving
   Skills in the Primary School Context
SO JOURNAL FOR THE EDUCATION OF THE GIFTED
LA English
DT Article
DE gifted children; social problem-solving; friendship relationships;
   psychological well-being
ID ADOLESCENTS; DEFINITIONS; SUPPORT
AB Gifted and typically developing children exhibit some differences in their developmental processes. This study compares the friendship relationships, psychological well-being, and social problem-solving skills of these two groups. The participants included 526 primary school children, comprising 241 gifted and 285 typically developing children. Data were collected using scales that measured friendship, psychological well-being, and social problem-solving skills and analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test. The results showed a significant difference in friendship scores, favoring typically developing children. Conversely, a significant difference in social problem-solving skills was found in favor of gifted children. No statistically significant difference was observed between the groups in terms of psychological well-being. These findings contribute to the growing body of research on gifted and typically developing children.

TI Understanding the roles of interest and self-efficacy in the processes
   of complex problem solving: Evidence from PISA 2012
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Complex problem solving; Problem exploration; Knowledge application;
   Interest; Self-efficacy
ID ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; PREDICTORS; MOTIVATION; INTELLIGENCE; MATHEMATICS;
   EXPLORATION; PERFORMANCE; ENGAGEMENT; CREATIVITY; BELIEFS
AB Complex problem solving (CPS) is a 21st-century competency that is an essential requirement for adolescents' success. Due to the complexity and dynamism of real-world problems, successful CPS demands effective exploration, information integration, as well as solutions generation, evaluation and application. And it contains both cognitive and noncognitive components. The relationship between cognitive components and CPS has been widely recognized, but the relationship between noncognitive components and CPS remains to be explored. Given that CPS comprises three distinguishable processes, namely problem exploration, representation and knowledge application, it is worth to examine the effects of noncognitive factors-anxiety, interest, selfefficacy, and self-concept-on the three CPS processes. Thus, the current study aimed to address this gap. A total of 5018 students from China (four regions), Australia, Brazil, the United States, and Norway who participated in the computer-based Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2012 assessment were selected. Binary logistic regression models were constructed to explore the interested relationships. The results highlight the importance of problem exploration and the difficulty of knowledge application. Moreover, interest contributes to effective problem exploration in China (four regions) and Australia, and promotes knowledge application in the United States and Norway. Self-efficacy is linked to problem representation in China (four regions) and Brazil. This study provides evidence for enhancing CPS through cultivating interest and self-efficacy, as well as reflects the necessity that interventions should be adjusted based on cultural and educational environments.

TI The use of Science Comics as a New Means to Promote Science in Adult
   Education: A Case Study
SO ADULT LEARNING
LA English
DT Article

   engagement
ID COMMUNICATION; BOOKS
AB Technical subjects in science may be difficult to understand because of the abstract nature of the relevant concepts. Alternative forms of teaching material are used to overcome this. One such form is comics, a popular art form providing a more relaxed environment, which has been used in various education setups with encouraging results. Although such novel forms are generally attractive to younger generations familiar with visual information, few studies have focused on their effect on adult learners. In this paper, several instances of the use of science comics in various setups are presented, showing that comics can provide a useful alternative way of education. Furthermore, their interest in learning other science subjects was enhanced and they expressed increased preference for an extended use of science comics in their education.

TI An Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Virtual Laboratory for
   Optoelectronics Education Using the Transfer Matrix Method
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial Intelligence tutor; optoelectronics education; solar cells;
   transfer matrix method; virtual laboratory
AB Visualizing sub-wavelength optical phenomena, such as thin-film interference and parasitic absorption, remains a significant pedagogical challenge in optoelectronics education. Furthermore, traditional physical laboratories require costly equipment, limiting student accessibility. To address these barriers, this study presents an interactive, MATLAB-based virtual laboratory designed to teach solar cell optics using the transfer matrix method (TMM). The software enables students to construct standard multi-layer architectures (e.g., ITO/PEDOT:PSS/Active Blend/TiO2/Al) and immediately visualize critical optical outputs, including the electric field distribution |E(z)|2, spatial generation rate G(z), and macroscopic spectral reflectance. While traditional simulators provide mathematical outputs, they function as unguided platforms, leaving students to interpret dense graphical data alone. To bridge the gap between complex optical data and physical intuition, the defining novelty of this virtual laboratory is the integration of a multimodal, context-aware Artificial Intelligence (AI) tutor powered by a Large Language Model (LLM). This embedded assistant dynamically processes both numerical parameters and rasterized visual plots to guide students through Socratic questioning and engineering design critiques. Enriched by 2D and 3D parameter sweeps and a comparative case manager to explore the short-circuit current density (J sc) optimization landscape, this platform merges rigorous computational physics with automated pedagogical guidance to cultivate practical design skills in next-generation semiconductor engineers.

TI Does the Double Reduction Policy Mitigate the Academic Gaps Caused by
   SES and Urban-Rural Settings?
SO EDUCATION AND URBAN SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE academic achievement gap; socioeconomic status; urban-rural context;
   double reduction policy
AB How to effectively reduce academic disparities and promote educational equity has attracted much attention in recent years. Introduced in China in 2021, the Double Reduction Policy (DRP) seeks to advance fairness in education, yet its effectiveness remains widely debated. This study critically examines the implications of the DRP, focusing on its role in narrowing achievement gaps across socioeconomic groups and between urban-rural students, as well as its impact on equalizing educational outcomes. Using national data from the Chinese Family Panel Studies (CFPS) for 2020 and 2022, a quantitative comparative approach is employed to assess policy effects. Statistical analyses explore variations across socioeconomic and regional contexts. The findings indicate that the DRP has contributed to reducing urban-rural disparities (narrowed by 0.283, p < .01) and weakening the influence of socioeconomic status (SES) on achievement (SES & times; Policy = -0.363, p < .01). Yet, parents continue to assume that family and school influences are the most significant for their children's performance, regardless of what the evidence shows as an equalizer. Hence, notable inequalities persist offering important insights for advancing equity-oriented and sustainable reforms.

TI Identifying Diverse Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence Among
   Middle School Students Through Latent Profile Analysis
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE attitudes towards artificial intelligence; computational identity;
   latent profile analysis; middle school students; scale adaption
ID PROGRAMMING EMPOWERMENT; COMPUTATIONAL IDENTITY; ONLINE; PREDICTORS;
   COMPONENTS; ENGAGEMENT; MODEL
AB This study aims to determine the student profiles of middle school students by examining their attitudes towards artificial intelligence (ATAI) and their computational identity (CI) structures. CI, which can be considered a domain-specific form of cognitive identity in programming and AI contexts, was examined in four basic dimensions such as participation in programming, belonging, realization, and goal setting. The study examined ATAI as cognitive, affective, and behavioural components. The data obtained from 453 students studying in middle school in Turkey were evaluated with latent profile analysis (LPA). As a result of the study, it was found that the short form of the AI attitude scale also presented strong construct validity. On the other hand, three different student profiles were revealed according to LPA. Profile 1 represents students with a low level of AI attitude and a low level of cognitive identity, while Profile 2 consists of students with a high level of attitude and cognitive identity. Profile 3, on the other hand, consists of students who are in between these two groups and have medium level values. The multinomial logistic regression analysis was conducted as a supplementary within-model comparison to examine how ATAI and CI components are structurally associated with profile differentiation, rather than to establish predictive relationships. The findings indicated that CI components represent the primary dimensions along which the profiles differ. On the other hand, demographic variables such as age, gender, or AI experience were not significantly associated with profile membership.

TI Exploring the Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in
   Research Activities in Shaping Doctoral Students' Well-Being
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE doctoral education; doctoral students' well-being; generative AI;
   psychological well-being; self-determination theory
ID SATURATION; INTERVIEWS
AB This qualitative study explores the implications of generative AI (GenAI) use in research for doctoral students' psychological well-being and the associated disciplinary differences. It draws on Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and interviews with 20 PhD students from diverse disciplines at a Chinese university. Findings reveal an overall positive picture: GenAI use in research can enhance doctoral students' psychological well-being by boosting competence-through greater efficiency and less time pressure-and reinforcing autonomy via a stronger sense of empowerment and leadership. It also fosters relatedness by promoting secure attachment. Different patterns and nuances were identified across disciplines regarding senses of empowerment and the related sense of efficiency and leadership. Moreover, our findings caution that overusing GenAI in research may amplify peer pressure and compel doctoral students to engage in a publication rat race, worsening their well-being. Overall, this paper highlights GenAI as a potential well-being enabler for doctoral students and offers practical implications for universities.

TI Making Thinking Visible in the English Language Classroom: Insights From
   Secondary School Teachers in Malaysia
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE English language education; Malaysian secondary education; thinking
   skills; thinking tools; visible thinking routines
ID PEDAGOGY; PERCEPTIONS; STUDENTS
AB A narrative of 'deficit' and 'lack' seem to represent Malaysian students as thinkers. In response, we were interested in exploring how teachers utilised Visible Thinking Routines (VTRs) to prompt, scaffold and support thinking among students in English language classrooms. Data were collected over a nine-month period in two phases. Sixty-five open-ended survey responses and eight interviews were analysed thematically and three prominent themes emerged. First, teachers perceived VTRs as the 'right tool for the job', recognising their suitability in fostering thinking skills. Second, positive shifts in students' thinking and engagement were observed, with VTRs enabling more active participation, creativity and thoughtful responses. Finally, teachers identified balancing time constraints with deep thinking goals a challenge. Success stories can create 'buy-in' to encourage others to consider this tool to promote thinking. If more teachers make thinking central to teaching, then more positive reports on Malaysian students as thinkers may surface, replacing the current narrative of 'lack' and 'deficit'.

TI An Extended Technology Acceptance Model to Explain Higher Education
   Students' Behavioral Intention to Use ChatGPT: The Case of Kazakhstan
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; behavioral patterns; ChatGPT; higher education;
   technology acceptance model
ID PERCEIVED EASE; DRIVERS; SEM
AB The present study aimed to model university students' behavioral intention in Kazakhstan to use ChatGPT for academic purposes, based on the extended technology acceptance model (TAM), and to examine correlations among variables expected to influence behavioral intention. A quantitative research method was employed in this study, which involved 200 higher education students. In addition to the main TAM components-perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and behavioral intention (BI)-five exogenous variables, which included subjective norm (SNM), school influence (SIE), peer influence (PIE), perceived enjoyment (PEN), and AI self-efficacy (AISE), were included in the research model. The partial least squares structural equation model (PLS-SEM) was utilized to analyze the proposed model. The proposed model provided a good fit for explaining BI among university students in Kazakhstan and accounted for 50.3% of the variance in BI. It was determined that perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, along with the exogenous variables, are direct and indirect predictors of BI. The theoretical and practical implications of using ChatGPT for academic support were discussed in the study.

TI SRL Components Predicting Math Results in Estonian Middle School: A
   Bayesian Analysis
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Bayesian networks; cognition; conceptual math knowledge; motivation
   procedural and factual math knowledge and skills; self-regulated
   learning
ID COGNITIVE PREDICTORS; MATHEMATICS; KNOWLEDGE; ACHIEVEMENT; SKILLS;
   COVARIATION; VALIDITY
AB Self-regulated learning (SRL) components, such as motivation, cognitive skills and learning strategies, play a critical role in mathematics (math) learning. Using Bayesian Networks (BN), this study examines which SRL components predict membership in high (75th percentile) and low-performing (25th percentile) groups in factual/procedural and conceptual math among middle school students (N = 658). The results revealed that cognitive skills-specifically identifying key information in texts, scientific thinking and attention-were direct predictors of factual/procedural and conceptual knowledge. Self-efficacy also emerged as a consistent motivational predictor across all models. Quick and frequent help-seeking during tasks was found to predict belonging to a group of low conceptual knowledge, while text comprehension and working memory were specifically related to factual/procedural skills. Indirect influences among SRL components were also identified. The study highlights how different SRL variables contribute to various dimensions of mathematical competence and contrasts the most influential predictors of belonging to either high- or low-achieving student groups.

TI Policy Dialogue: DEI, Culture Wars, and the History of Education
SO HISTORY OF EDUCATION QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
AB The recent surge of attacks on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) has prompted urgent questions about the past, present, and future of such initiatives. In this HEQ policy dialogue, Kevin Kumashiro and Michael Olneck take up those questions directly, tracing how contemporary assaults-beginning with criticisms of the 1619 Project, critical race theory, and gender studies-have broadened into a campaign aimed at reshaping curriculum, institutions, and civic understanding. They probe the power of narrative and counter-narrative, asking what stories about democracy, citizenship, and education are being advanced and whether progressive educators and advocates have offered compelling alternatives.Drawing on historical examples and political theory, their conversation situates today's moment within longer struggles over who belongs in the American civic imaginary-from early twentieth-century immigrant restrictionism to competing visions of liberty voiced in nineteenth-century abolitionist and Reconstruction debates. Kumashiro and Olneck consider how new social imaginaries are articulated and disseminated, and what educators might do to cultivate aspirations about the kind of society and schools we aim to build.Michael Olneck is Professor Emeritus in the departments of Educational Policy Studies and Sociology at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and the author of Culture Wars in American Education: Past and Present Struggles Over the Symbolic Order, along with numerous articles and book chapters on multiculturalism in American education. TI Proportional Relations When Programming Using Scratch: The Case of
   Pre-Service Elementary School Teachers
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Abstraction; Computational thinking; Direct and inverse relations;
   Mathematical thinking; Scratch
ID COMPUTATIONAL THINKING; EDUCATION
AB Programming activities provide learners with opportunities to implement both computational and mathematical thinking while developing abstraction, which lies at the core of both domains. Although abstraction is fundamental to both computational and mathematical thinking, it is conceptualized and interpreted differently in each, as explained below. This study examines changes in level of abstract thinking among 41 pre-service elementary school teachers as they use the Scratch environment to produce animations in sequence of six tasks. These tasks were designed to provide repeated opportunities for abstracting proportional relations, including direct and inverse relations between motion and time. To analyze the data, we defined three levels of abstraction that capture these relations in the scripts of each task. We examined the extent to which pre-service elementary school teachers' scripts demonstrated shifts in levels of abstraction across the sequence of programming tasks. The findings reveal gradual shifts in pre-service elementary school teachers' levels of abstraction for both direct and inverse relations. This study extends prior research on the relations between computational and mathematical abstract thinking by focusing on proportional relations and offering a novel approach for assessing levels of abstraction in programming.

TI Person-Directed Staffing and Quality of Life: Links Between Staff
   Choice, Perceived Staff Stability and Community Participation for
   Individuals With IDD in the United States
SO JOURNAL OF APPLIED RESEARCH IN INTELLECTUAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE choice; community inclusion; intellectual disability; National Core
   Indicators; staff stability
ID DIRECT SUPPORT PROFESSIONALS; NATIONAL CORE INDICATORS;
   DEVELOPMENTAL-DISABILITIES; INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY; ADULTS; WORKFORCE;
   PEOPLE; WAGES
AB Background and Aims Direct support professionals (DSPs) are essential to individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD), yet staff turnover remains a significant concern. This study examined whether individuals with IDD in the United States are involved in choosing their staff, how they perceive staff turnover and whether perceived staff stability is associated with quality of life.Methods Data from the 2022-2023 National Core Indicators-In Person Survey were analysed to assess relationships between staff choice, perceived staff stability and outcomes related to everyday choice, support-related choice and alignment of community activities with personal preferences.Results Individuals involved in choosing their staff were more likely to report greater staff stability. Perceived staff stability was associated with better alignment between community participation and personal preferences but was not significantly associated with choice-making outcomes.Conclusion Findings support person-directed service models and highlight the value of involving individuals with IDD in staffing decisions to promote staff stability and person-centred community participation.

TI Agency Under Constraint: Everyday Negotiations of Motherhood Among Women
   With Intellectual Disabilities in Yogyakarta, Indonesia
SO JOURNAL OF APPLIED RESEARCH IN INTELLECTUAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE agency; intellectual disability; motherhood; parenting capacity;
   relational autonomy; social work
AB Objective Mothers with intellectual disabilities are frequently positioned within deficit-oriented and ableist discourses that question their parenting capacity. While recent scholarship has increasingly foregrounded lived experiences, limited attention has been given to how agency is exercised within relational and hierarchical family contexts, particularly outside high-income Western settings. This study examines how mothers with intellectual disabilities in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, negotiate motherhood under conditions of stigma and family regulation.Methods A qualitative interpretive design was employed involving in-depth interviews with three mothers with intellectual disabilities in Yogyakarta, complemented by contextual interviews with family members and disability advocates, as well as participant observation. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, drawing on an integrated framework of stigma theory, relational autonomy, everyday resistance and ethics of care.Results Three themes emerged inductively: negotiating reproductive decisions, negotiating maternal legitimacy and strategic silence and everyday care. The women actively negotiated reproductive decisions, maternal legitimacy and everyday caregiving through strategic timing of pregnancy disclosure, refusal of coerced abortion, insistence on marriage, selective silence and sustained involvement in their children's education and protection-enacting agency within structural constraint.Conclusion These findings challenge independence-based interpretations of parenting capacity and demonstrate how agency and vulnerability coexist. By presenting evidence from a Southeast Asian collectivist context, the study extends existing literature beyond its predominantly Western focus. A relational autonomy perspective provides a culturally grounded framework for understanding parenting among women with intellectual disabilities and has important implications for social work practice.

TI Previous Experiences of Discrimination Impact College Students' Mental
   Health and Treatment Outcomes at University Counseling Centers
SO JOURNAL OF COUNSELING PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE counseling; discrimination; minoritized identities; treatment outcome;
   intersectionality
ID MINORITY STRESS; SOCIAL STRESS; INTERSECTIONALITY; STIGMA;
   PSYCHOTHERAPY; DISPARITIES; VALIDATION; SYMPTOMS; TRAUMA; GENDER
AB Despite efforts to improve diversity, equity, inclusion, and belonging on college campuses in recent years, students with minority statuses (i.e., stigmatized identities based on race, gender, sexual orientation, nationality, disability, religion, etc.) continue to encounter identity-based discrimination. A robust body of literature has established that discriminatory experiences are related to poor mental health and academic outcomes in minoritized college students. However, among students who decide to seek treatment, it remains unclear how discrimination experiences might contribute to presenting distress and treatment outcomes. The present study used multivariate analyses to examine the differences in multiple domains of psychological symptoms at intake and at the end of treatment between students who reported discriminatory experiences in the past 6 months compared to those who did not. Data were collected through the Center for Collegiate Mental Health between July 2021 and June 2023 (N = 45,778). At intake, students who experienced discrimination reported more severe psychological symptoms, including suicidal ideation, compared to students who did not experience discrimination. These students also experienced less reduction in academic distress and internalized symptoms (i.e., depression and anxiety) at the end of treatment. Importantly, when clients experienced discrimination against multiple versus a singular facet of their identity (e.g., race and gender), the negative impact on their baseline symptoms was amplified, but this effect was not found in treatment outcome. We discuss the clinical implications of these findings and future directions for research and clinical practice in light of intersectionality theory.
